utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. I notice that for the record, that all the accused are present. Same applies to the Defence teams, except that I don't see Mr. Bourgon. Ms. Nikolic, will he show up later on or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Bourgon will be working in the office, working on the submissions that we have announced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And for the Prosecution I notice Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Baraybar, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Please proceed with the solemn undertaking to testify the truth that you -- is being handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll skip all preliminaries in an attempt to try to finish your testimony today. Mr. McCloskey -- please make yourself comfortable. Mr. McCloskey will examine you in direct, and then he will be followed by cross-examinations. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon everyone, and this will be very brief on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you first state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My name is Jose Pablo Baraybar do Carmo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you testified previously in this Srebrenica case, in the case of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your testimony there true and correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you had been asked those same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, they will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you briefly outline your educational background that led you to that field?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My first degree is in archaeology, that -- I took it in Peru, at the University of San Marcos in Lima. I took a Master's in science at the University College of London in a combination of bioarchaeology, physical anthropology, and forensics. I did one year at the Ph.D. programme at the University of Champaign-Urbana, the department of anthropology, and I am currently doing my Ph.D. at the University of Strasbourg, in science as well as, in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Champaign-Urbana is near Chicago?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: South of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you outline your field work as an forensic pathologist and archaeologist, given, as you know this Court has had some -- quite a bit of experience and testimony on these basic subjects. So if you could just outline your field work?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My work has spanned from recovery, recording, and analysis of human remains in the contexts where they were found, meaning graves, mass graves, multiple graves, single graves, in Haiti, Ethiopia, Sierra Leone, Congo, Rwanda, Guatemala, Argentina, Peru, the Balkans, or this Tribunal has understood, meaning Bosnia, Croatia, Kosovo. That is very much it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many years have you been doing this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: For the UN alone, since 1995, and before the UN, since 1991, specifically in forensic settings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you now briefly outline your UN work, beginning in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I started the United Nations mission in Haiti, back then. From then I went to ICTR, to International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. From then we were transferred along to ICTY, for six weeks that became a few years. In 2002 I left ICTY and became the head of the office on missing persons and forensics in Kosovo for UNMIK, the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, where I am still based at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to just briefly focus your attention now on when you were, as you said, I think, briefly loaned to Bosnia. Can you tell us, outline your work that -- in Bosnia, when and where?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I will tell you in general terms because I cannot really recall exactly how many sites we did all over the years. In Rwanda we were part of what was called, if I recall correctly, the scientific support unit of the Office of the Prosecutor. This unit as a whole was lent to ICTY to start at the time the investigations, forensic investigation on the fall of Srebrenica. That we started, if I'm not mistaken, by the end of June, early July, 1996. During that year we did a number of exhumations and post-mortem examinations as well, in Bosnia, as well as Croatia, because in Croatia it was also the exhumation of the site at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the site at Ovcara, was that related to the Vukovar, the attack on Vukovar case?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And your work in the Srebrenica case in 1996, what position did you have on that -- during that -- on that team?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: From a UN point of view, I were a junior forensic anthropologist or forensic expert employed by the Tribunal. There were two people of technical expertise at the Tribunal at the time, it was Dr. Bill Haglund and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then just continue your brief outline through the years?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: So 1996 was a year primarily devoted to a case, it would be Srebrenica, and Ovcara or the fall of Vukovar case. 1997 we had -- if I am not mistaken, Brcko, there was another case, I think -- I don't want to recall exactly who the accused were, but it was another investigation. 1998 primarily devoted to Srebrenica again, extensively. 1999 a combination of cases, Srebrenica and some other case in Croatia. Year 2000, I spent it in Kosovo primarily and in other investigations regarding the northwest part of Bosnia, primarily crimes committed in the Prijedor area. 2001, again Srebrenica, and Croatia as well; there is yet another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I am really want to just take you to the time that you had a supervisory job, and I don't want to go through each time you were a supervisor, I think that's probably clear in the record and the reports. But can you tell us generally the position you held as a supervisor? And I think the Court has heard, I believe that -- well, I'll let you answer that question. In what areas were you a supervisor in?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Primarily from 1997 on I was the chief anthropologist at the mortuary dealing with a number of other contractors, anthropologists as well working in the mortuary in the analysis of skeletal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. And just very briefly, what in just a couple of sentences, is your job in the mortuary, in the analysis of remains?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to give you as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And not as a supervisor but as an anthropologist, what are the anthropologists doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The exhumation of graves, mass graves, primary graves, secondary graves in the former Yugoslavia and that is going beyond Srebrenica involved recovery of a number of decomposed or heavily decomposed remains, many of which were just skeletons, which is bones. In the case of secondary graves, where remains have been fragmented, they have become really body parts and pieces, they were primarily again bones with very little flesh, just bones. Therefore, the role of the anthropologist was to determine the age, sex, stature whenever pertinent, and also to estimate the minimum number of individuals based on the remains they have recovered. Also to assist in reconstruction of broken parts in order to determine the type of injury that this person has sustained whenever possible. For example, if a skull was broken in many pieces, you would need to ascertain whether the skull has been broken because of the pressure of the earth over it or has been shot on the head, for example. And the only way you can do it is by reconstructing it and then discussing the results with a pathologist, that is a person who ascertains the cause of death at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Does this include an anthropologist expertise on identifying potential trauma on bones?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely. Most definitely. Forensic pathologist on a daily basis confronted actually with that. The issue is not only to receive bones and say that the bones are human, is to try to say as much as you can from them, meaning what is the age, sex, et cetera, but also what happened to them. So if there is any kind of fracture or something that is broken, you try to establish what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just give you one example. I've seen reports where anthropologist say that marks on the bones are -- appear to be from scavenging animals. How can you tell the difference between teeth marks of an animal and scratch marks from something else?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There is a subdiscipline of archaeology that is called zooarchaeology, that is actually archaeologists working with animal or fauna remains from archaeological assemblages. So there is a tremendous body of information collected on what are the patterns and marks and evidence of scavenging by animals. That's one level. There is a number of other studies made to determine what are the patterns of scavenging by different kinds of animals. So, for example, a rodent that have permanent anterior teeth that grow forever, they have to keep, I mean, chewing or gnawing on something in order to keep wearing these teeth down, otherwise the teeth will be enormous. They are very clear differences. I do not want to go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And, again, now, let's go back to the morgue, your job as a supervisor. Can you tell us, fundamentally, what your job as a supervising anthropologist was, just very briefly. Again, I think, this is in the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Primarily try to give some consistency to the analysis that will be undertaken. In some occasions we had a lot of people, I mean over a dozen experts working simultaneously in different autopsy tables and the way they were recording things has to be protocolised, the types of forms that we use has to be protocolised as well. We try to be as consistent as possible in -- in recording things. Also because, based on that information, we will be able later to calculate things like the minimum number of individuals, for example. So primarily that, trying to ensure consistency and continuity, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about working with pathologists?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As well. Certainly my role as supervisor was, as they say, added value. I was not literally, like, standing, supervising people from a higher ground; rather working with them. It's just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whose job was it to determine cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It has always been the pathologist. The pathologist has a prerogative of ascertaining the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you also lead digs or exhumations for the Srebrenica case and others?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Back in 1999 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, what was your role there and in which case or cases?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We assembled again a team of archaeologists to work in the field, and we were tasked with a number of exhumations of a number of sites, but I could mention the ones I recall on the top of my head, otherwise I have the reports here. Will be the Glogova 2 sites, the Novo Kasaba sites, there were some done in 1996, but we -- a number of others done later. Konjevic Polje, that was very close by. Zeleni Jadar as well, that was back in 2001, there were some secondary sites, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think the record will have the complete list, so that's fine. Now, I want to take you back to a topic that you mentioned briefly, and that is determining the minimal number of individuals. And in particular you had written a report several years ago, it's Exhibit P02477, which was accepted into evidence in the Blagojevic case, but through the testimony of a an investigator, Dean Manning, and your Krstic testimony came in through 92 bis. So you haven't testified about that report. And it's not my intention to have you go through that report in depth, but could you explain -- well, basically two -- two main points. What is this calculation, minimum number of individuals, as it's relating to a grave? And as I've said, the Court has heard lots of information about graves, secondary graves, loose bones, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. In the simplest of terms, a minimal number of individuals is a slightly more complicated head count. If we can just oversimplify it. If you have a grave with complete bodies you are going to count them and say, Okay, we have 10 people because we have 10 cadavers. If you have fragmentary material, pieces of people, how would you, I mean, try to estimate at least how many people were they to account for the number of bones you are seeing. That is the calculation of the minimum number of individuals. It consists of primarily of counting one of a pair or a single type of bone to say that at least, if I have, for example, 10 right legs, I've got 10 people. So it's a conservative, I mean, approach. This calculation becomes more and more complicated when you try to merge sites. So I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we get to merge sites, you say counting individual bones, legs. Why not just count skulls? Everybody's only got one skull.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In an ideal world you would have a complete skulls. In other experience is that, and was far from ideal, nothing was complete. You had literally pieces of people, very small pieces. So you could have half a person, or you would have just bits of people. Or you would have a mass of flesh that contains some bones in it, but to get to the bones you have to remove the flesh, and you cannot identify an organ or part of the body. Therefore, you have to go for whatever bone is more commonly occurring. So if the heads, as you were saying, are only 10 but I've got 20 legs, you're going to go for the legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you the person that was tasked with taking all these individual bones and pieces of bones and trying to figure out for all the graves a minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, how can you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to explain it in the simplest terms again. Although if -- if at some point you don't understand what I'm saying, please interrupt me. I gave you the easiest example, okay, the leg count, for example. But I mean you would be assuming that the leg would be complete. So if we understand that the leg is composed by three bones, you've got the femur, that is your thigh, then the shin bone that compose two other bones, the tibula and fibula, if we focus on the femur to begin with, what would happen if your femur is actually divided into two or three pieces? Okay? You would need to choose what part of the bone you would be using to count as a single element; the top part or the bottom part, okay? So for example, in site A we have counted the proximal, the top part of the femur of 50 individuals, so a MNI, minimal number of individuals is 50. We have now another site, okay, for example a secondary site where the femur was not the most abundant bone, it was the arm bone. The humerus. And there we counted, for example, 20 top parts, proximal parts of humerus. You would say, okay, the MNI is 70, 50 plus 20 is 70, that is not correct. In order to do an MNI of the merged sites you need to be counting the same type of bone. So it is possible that in your second site, while the humerus tells you 20, the same part of the femur you counted in the previous site is only 10. So you would be -- you would be cutting off your calculation 10 individuals, that will become invisible. The MNI of these two merged sites would become 60 and not 70. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do you subtract 10?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Because you're not counting the same type of bone. You have to be -- the only condition is for you to count the same type of bone in both sites. You cannot count -- you cannot just simply add the numbers, you would be inflating the numbers. You would not be the minimal number of individuals, it would be something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I read you well, why count 10 and not go outright to zero because at this point in time you wouldn't be sure whether any of those bones belonged to the same individuals whose humerus or whose femur you -- you counted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me rephrase what I'm trying to explain. May I show you some -- may I show you some -- actually, this -- since we exhibited already in the Krstic trial, I don't know whether I can show some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, and you can use the ELMO, as you have done before. I think we have a P0553, and somehow Janet has figured out that that's what you've got.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: This is the ideal scenario we mentioned at the beginning, okay. We have two -- I mean, lower leg, forearms in this case. I'm sorry. Two forearms that are articulated, therefore we have two people. There are no problems. We are just doing, you know, a straightforward count. There's no problem there. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second to throw in just another element that it may be easier to work it in now than it is later. You oversaw exhumations, this Court has heard about exhumations, and disturbed exhumations, and it's very clear, as you know, that when a -- one of these graves is being partially exhumed, bodies are getting cut in pieces, and -- and perhaps multiple pieces, and hauled away at either the -- near the same time or at other times, and therefore there's certainly I think everyone understands the possibility that a person's body parts get separated into more than one secondary grave. So with that in mind, how do you work that into this whole calculation? If you agree with me, what I said factually about a person getting hacked up into more graves than just one?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is completely true. So before I go to the next image, and bearing in mind what you just said, the issue is the following: Let's just start from the beginning maybe just to -- for clarity's sake. We have a grave, people are killed and are buried in a grave, they're complete. There's nothing -- no factors have influenced the finding -- integrity of the remains. We've got -- and we have a hundred bodies in a hole. If that is the case, we just count the hundred bodies and there's no problem. There is no minimal number of anything, it's just the number we have, a finite number, a hundred. We get back to this site, X number of time or month after, with a machine, an excavator, and we removed, I mean in any blind way, I mean without any system, we just, like, start excavating and getting bodies out and put them in a truck. This machine will cut through bodies and will separate, will disjoint them, will cut them in half on the head, on the arm, doesn't matter. It's a completely haphazard way of doing it. This grave with a hundred will then become five secondary sites with bits and pieces of the hundred. So certainly it is highly likely that you will have one person which remains which may be in the first grave and then in the other five grave, okay. So in order to get the minimal number of people present in all the graves, the primary and the secondaries, you have -- for consistency, you need to count the same type of bone. Otherwise you will be duplicating them. And this is what I was saying about the 20 and the 10. If the most popular bone, for example, in the primary site is the right femur, you will be counting only right femur in all the other sites, because then you know you have X number of right femur and X number of individuals. Even if by chance one of the holes contain only arms and we have all two arms, you have 200 arms in one -- in one single hole, you may say Oh, this is more abundant, let's just count them there, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the hole with only 200 arms and no femurs gets a minimal number of what?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Obviously the 200 arms, that was an exaggeration, you may be able to get your MNI, I mean, based on only that secondary site because there are no arms in any other place. That is extreme and I have never seen such a thing. That is an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What, did you use one particular sort of bone for all of these graves or how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, just to make matters more complicated, the issue that we are looking at is not only numbers, we are looking also at ages, okay. If you have, in a previous example, a hundred right femur of adults, you know that you have a hundred adult people, at least a hundred adult people there. But what would happen if you find an arm bone that is this size and not that size, meaning the size of an individual that may be 12 years of age or maybe eight years of age. But there is no femur for that -- for that child. So you have to count that individual as well, even if you are using a different type of bone. Because there is a different age that is not represented by the bones you have used for the calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But how -- how good are these age estimations? I don't want to go into all the science of that that you talk about, but they're -- from what I see, they're pretty big ranges.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There are two different things when you work with human remains. Whether to be accurate or whether to be precise. In order to be precise, you have to give an interval that is extremely short. For example any technique that determines the age with a deviation, a margin on the sides of the estimate of, let's say, one or two years is fantastic. You say this person is 10.5 years, you know, plus, minus one, well, that's excellent. But this -- I mean, doesn't really occur in reality. Because age determination is multi-factoral. You have count many different things in order to determine the age of one person. You begin by looking at the bone and saying, Oh, this person is, you know, that age. You say, Okay, it is an adult or no. It's a juvenile or whatever. So the widest your range, you know, allows you to be less precise but more accurate. In other words, just [indiscernible] me for a second, the extreme of this is every person in this room is between zero and 100 years of age. I'm always accurate, I am 100 per cent accurate, but I am very unprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But in your science what -- how close can you get, and still would be within a reasonable range? What is the reasonable age range that you in your science in this context of Bosnia could be? What were the age ranges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It doesn't to me. Excuse me, I do not understand your question. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How close can you get to the person who --

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: To the real age of the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In order to verify that, we would need to compare our results with people that have been identified, now identified. That's number one. Number two, there is a second way to approach this problem, and that is to compare the distribution of age of the bodies exhumed with the distribution of age of the people reported missing from this event to which these bodies belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But just -- just on the science of anthropology, I have seen in the reports, in individual anthropology report, for example, age, and it says 12 to 17 years old, something like that. How does -- how do you come up with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. Now I can answer your question. I understand it better now. The age determination of any person below, let's say 21, 22, it is much easier to be established than the age of people 20 something, let's say 25 and above. Why? When you grow, you have a number of elements in your body that are fusing to one another, I'm using very simple language to be understood. For example, if I may use this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may just be simpler just to talk.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If I may steal, I wanted to show -- I mean, can you just can point something here on -- on this -- on this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Can I -- no, I cannot draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You have parts of bones like this one or like this one or like this one that are called epiphyses, that when the person -- when the person is bone, actually the bone is primarily a cartilage model that has only a tiny centre of ossification of bone that is located generally in the middle part of the bone, the rest is cartilage. So the bone is growing in this direction and in that direction. So this little parts, we call epiphyses, do fuse with the remaining of the bone before age 21 in general terms. In females it is faster, in males it is slower, and these allow you him a high degree of accuracy and more precision, certainly to determine age in people below the early 20s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so the age ranges in your reports above the early 20s, do you think they reflect, those are fair ages despite the problems you talk about?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The fair age range is, for the type of material we have been confronted, for example, if you have a piece of a leg, and you can just identify that it is a piece of a leg, a piece of a femur bone, or you have, let's say, again in this example, you have this piece of the bone, well, you can say, Okay, this is a forearm, I have a radius and an ulnar here, it is most likely an adult individual, but whether this person is 22 and a half or 35, I cannot say. Therefore, we have a very wide range of 25 plus of all those numbers of people that were just represented by pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And your reports will reflect that wide range?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's finish up with this. If you could just initial -- initial this thing and date this so that we can freeze it and keep track of it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That or here? [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think we're okay with that for now. Now, let's -- I diverted you to age or you talked about age as you were explaining the minimal number and how that also helped yet complicated your calculation. But I still -- well, you haven't had the chance yet to really be able to explain how, with these multiple graves with body parts like this, the secondary graves, how did you do it, did you use one bone for all the graves or were there different graves where different bones were used?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Rather the second. I mean, different graves will have different bones. But the first condition, in order to merge anything, is to know what are you merging. Meaning you have to be sure that a primary and a secondary site are related and that will not come -- will not be bone evidence, that will be soil analysis, pollen analysis, all sorts of other analysis. Once you have established that a primary site is linked to one or multiple secondary sites, then you can go on the bone issue to see what type of bone you would use and what bones may be representing ages not represented by your most common bone, as I said at beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And were you able to have access in this calculation that we talked about in this report from the investigations as well as from the sciences, such as pollen analysis or shell casing analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The only access I had, and that is in my report, if I recall well, are primarily data concerning a soil analysis and I think pollen as well, that was Dr. Brown work. But I'm going through, if you allow me for a second, through my reports to see that what I'm saying is totally accurate. But it was primarily -- primarily that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the value of your minimum number is really dependent on the quality of the information you get relating graves to each other. If that's wrong, it's going to mess up your records -- or your calculations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's about as far as I want to go. If anyone else would like to, I turn the witness over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I have three Defence teams that have indicated that they do not wish to cross-examine the witness. That's the Nikolic, Borovcanin, and Gvero teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Confirmed on behalf of the General Gvero, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can also confirm that we have no cross for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I can confirm that we won't be needing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there is another arrangement reached between you, I would suggest that Mr. Haynes -- yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just indicate we don't have any cross-examination for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's Mr. Haynes who has asked for two hours, and Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Meek have 45 minutes, and then you, Madam Fauveau, 10 minutes. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Hi, how are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very well. I hope you are too. Can I just check one thing before we proceed any further. I've got no difficulty with this. You've got some documents in front of you. I assume they are your reports. Do you have any other documents in front of you that I should know about?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not that I plan to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Don't need to know about newspapers or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, no. I've got some scientific articles, but, I mean, I have them in my pile of papers but nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I want to see if I can help you, because I've looked quite carefully at your involvement in the Srebrenica case, and I thoroughly understand that when you are exhuming graves all over Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia, you don't necessarily remember them all, but I want to see if I can summarise your involvement in the graves that we're concerned with. You will know from the tables in your report that there are 30 graves we're concerned with. You would agree with that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: 30 graves dug in general, you mean, by ICTY, not by me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I'm going come to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, you may be right. I don't have the table of all the graves exhumed in front of me, but it may be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you want to check it, you can look at page 7 or 8 of your minimum number of individuals report. I'm not going throw it up on e-court. You can just check that figure.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That would be the report of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I have it in front of me here. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'll try and put it chronologically, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In 1996, you assisted Mr. Haglund in the exhumation of four sites. They were Cerska, Nova Kasaba, Lazete 2 and Branjevo or Pilica, as we know it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in the exhumations there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In 1998 you assisted Mr. Wright in the excavation of a number of sites at Hodzici Road, Cancari Road, Zeleni Jadar, the Red Dam, and Liplje?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in most of those exhumations too, and I say most because at the time I also spent some periods in the -- in the mortuary. So one of the Hodzici Road sites I participated, I think, in only one of the two. I mean, I cannot really recall exactly, but I mean most of what you are saying is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, one of the nice courtesies we as professional people have, is we thank one another for helping the report, so we can cross-reference who was working with who where. And I agree with you, you assisted Mr. Wright in most but not all, A, because you are in the mortuary and, B, because in 1999 when he was also working, you were in control of sites yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, but when I took control of the sites, if I recall well, Mr. Wright was not doing any exhumation. I mean, that is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue with you about that, it's not really very important. In 1999 you excavated several sites yourself, that's Nova Kasaba 4 to 8, and Konjevic Polje 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in 2001 you excavated a number of sites at Glogova?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And one at Ravnice, maybe two. Do you recall whether you excavated more than one site at Ravnice or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I did not -- I have nothing to do with Ravnice at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well you have answered that particular conundrum for me. You had nothing to do with the exhumation of sites by Mr. Peccerelli?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And nothing to do with Ravnice and some of the sites excavated by Mr. Wright. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to check something with you before we go any further. Have you had chance before you give evidence here to read some of the reports of the other anthropologists and pathologists who have given evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, no. I have only mention -- or quoted data extracted from a pathology report in my previous archaeology report, primarily Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, and so on. But I have not read all the reports of all the conclusions or whatever, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to check the reports, I may be asking you about, have you read the reports of Mr. Haglund?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: From exhumations in 1996, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I have only taken the data attached to the -- I mean reports, the raw data primarily, the Excel sheets and so on, for the calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Wright?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about the pathologist, Mr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: From Clark I have extracted data, yes, as it is quoted in my reports. But I have not, I mean, read the report. I mean, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, having looked at the data and having been involved in, as it were, the anthropological investigation one way or another of most of these sites, can you tell us today the total number of complete bodies that were exhumed by the ICTY in relation to the Srebrenica investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: On the top of my head, I couldn't. As a matter of fact, we have certain sites that were primary sites that obviously the remains were complete or almost complete, as has been indicated as well in my reports, I do not have an overview of how many complete bodies and body parts we collected over the years. That's why we've been working primarily with minimum number of individuals. The reason for this being that since there were some very large sites, like Kozluk, for example, that was also robbed and part of the remains went to Cancari Road and the dam with Liplje and things of other kind, counting complete bodies wouldn't make much sense because you would have, as I said before, complete bodies left in the primary site and then pieces of the same remains in secondary sites linked to the primary sites. So, I mean, no, it wouldn't make any sense. And I do not have that information with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to push this any further at this stage. Are you saying that it is not possible for anybody to determine how many complete bodies were exhumed, or are you saying you just don't have the information with you here today?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I do not have information with me here today. It is possible to count how many bodies were found, if they were complete and were recorded as complete by the archaeologist in the field. That is completely possible, certainly. But I do not have that information with me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just this, while we're on this topic, in accordance with the protocols that you used, what was the definition of a complete body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is a very good point. And has been a lot of debate over that. Well, a complete body was primarily a unit that may lack some -- let's say the hands and the feet, but that most of it, the rest of them. I mean legs, I mean torso and arms, were present. And the head as well. At some point in time there was some internal discussion, and I'm just, like, recalling here, I cannot give you dates or anything of the kind, but I mean because it was very much work in progress, whether a body would be, for example, if you found a leg with a pelvis and half of the torso, would that be a body or would it be a body part, or a body part would be only an arm or a leg or a hand. My interpretation of complete bodies was primarily, I mean, something as recognisable of the body as possible. Meaning at least 75 or 80 per cent of what a body is made of would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know whether that's an interpretation of that description that was agreed with by Mr. Haglund, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what -- I mean what are you quoting from Mr. Haglund? If you have the quote there, you may ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to quote anything from him. But did he agree with your interpretation of what a complete body was?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not actually know. I mean, when I was recalling this issue of body parts, I recall the issue of body parts being discussed maybe in the context of -- of Mr. Wright. I mean to tell you the truth, I do not -- I'm really thinking very hard, to know whether I have discussed this issue of completeness of remains with -- with -- with Haglund or not. It was simply a -- an assumed -- I mean thing. I do not know. I don't recall, really, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your discussion with Mr. Wright, did that arise because the two of you had a different interpretation of what complete body meant?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not really. The problem is the following, just to put things into context, that would assist. Imagine that you have a number of experts working together and everybody had, obviously, I mean, may have opinions regarding things and that. So I -- I think that the discussion came in the context of a mapping, as a matter of fact, if I may being more precise. Because you may have heard, I mean, I think Mr. Wright already testified, he may have mentioned this, but we had a system of mapping with a total station that is a laser theodolite, anyway, for which you have to take a number of points. So the whole issue was whether you take a point at every -- I mean articulation like the wrist and the elbow and -- and the shoulder and things of that kind. And that had an impact on what a body part or a complete body was, because then where would you -- where do you stop measuring this? I mean, that is the context in which it happened, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I quite agree. And the reason I'm asking you for this is because it's a phrase that appears in the reports of all the pathologists in this case-, that the number of complete bodies recovered. But what I'm trying to explore with you, having been involved in the case from 1996 to 2001, is whether, during that period, it was a phrase that was used differently by each of them.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That I couldn't -- I couldn't tell you. What I can tell you for sure is that pathologists sometimes, and, again, I mean they didn't -- like a hundred of them, I could not tell you whom, would at some point in time, you know, maybe say okay, well this is -- I mean they opened the bag and said this is not a body part, it has to be a body because, I mean, there is a lot of -- you know, limbs and things here. So it has to be a body. And they may call it a body -- they change it from a BP, that was a call for a body part, to a body. But, I mean, it may have happened, yes. What I'm trying to say is that it was some kind of work in progress, I believe. But it may have happened, yes. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say it may have happened, you mean it may have happened that each of the pathologists in this case defined a complete body differently and a body part differently?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I wouldn't say that each of the pathologists. Remember that every --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did I say pathologist? I didn't mean pathologist, I meant anthropology [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, most definitely that wouldn't the case. That's why you had a supervisor of the team. Not every person would be calling whatever they saw in their own way. Obviously not. They could argue, give their reasons for it, but, I mean, they would be under the authority of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've given some evidence just now about, as it were, your role as supervisors and the protocols and procedure that is you had to oversee. Were the protocols and procedures constant throughout the period of 1996 to 2001 or could they change?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, they changed. I think that in 1996 all of this was quite new. It was very -- it was very. I mean the scale of everything was -- everybody was new. I think a lot was learned in the subsequent years after 1996 and things did change. And I would say they improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That implies that they were less than perfect in 1996. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about in 1998? Were they improved after 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I couldn't think the improvement hand only once, I think the improvement happened actually after -- every year, every season. Obviously, the point at the time was not just to reinvent the wheel after every season, because there would be no consistency, but there were areas that could be improved, I mean the logs, the observations, the types of things we were using for this and that. There was work in progress. There was an improvement of things. I mean, throughout. I mean, I would not just say 1998 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we may have to bounce back to that from time to time, but I want to get a rather more detailed picture, if I can, of how firstly a dig site was managed, and secondly how that coordinated with those who worked back at the morgue. There were a large number of staff at each of the dig sites, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would there have been anthropologists at the dig site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: When we -- yes. Yes. But just to clarify, in the American educational system people are trained as anthropologists, period. But anthropology for them has four subspecialties, linguists --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you. I think we've heard an abundance of evidence about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The answer is yes, Your Honour. I think he -- he was finishing his answer. He wasn't going to be long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I really didn't mean to be rude, but I think we know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish the answer, and then you can direct him to something different, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So to answer your question is yes, but bearing in mind that we should not be so rigid when we said we are the anthropologist or we are the archaeologist. Of course, we are both, a combination of both, but under the American educational system, for example, people would be called anthropologist, but they would be archaeologists, linguists, physical anthropologists or social, cultural anthropologists. So the answer is, yes, they mind that. In other systems, you may have a strict archaeologist trained in a department of archaeology, like in the U.K., for example, or even in Peru, for that matter. It is different in the American system. So the way they're referred to would be different, but in the case of anthropologists, it can imply archaeologist or physical anthropologist or forensic anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question is rather redundant now, but -- and there would be archaeologists at the site of a dig, as well, wouldn't there? Or collectively archaeologists/anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, would I like the stroke, yes. The stroke element is the most clarifying one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We will agree on that. Would you have a pathologist at a dig site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. We wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Scenes of crime technicians?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Investigators?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The investigating team -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And a large number of assistants, some of whom had nothing do with the criminal investigation, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In what context, again, I mean, you're referring this? 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah, in 1996 there were a large number of people who worked for the Physicians for Human Rights. They were not employed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, what I mean -- I mean, again, I will not comment on things I do not know first-hand because, yes, I was there, I do not know all the details regarding the contractual arrangements between the Tribunal and PHR or anything of the kind, but when you refer a large number of people, the way -- the way -- I mean, at the site, you mean? I mean, the way they at the site, at the mortuary, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I'm still at the dig site. I'm coming on to the mortuary. Were there people at the dig site who were not part of the process of the investigation of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, there were supporting staff, I mean logistic people, the backhoe driver, I mean the truck driver operating the refrigerated container. Certainly those people had nothing to do with the criminal investigation. But, again, I am unable to run a backhoe, or Dr. Haglund or whoever was over. Therefore, the support staff to a criminal investigation but not directly involved or participating in the criminal investigation as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about people working for human rights organisations, were they present at the dig sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: From -- I mean, what people?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I should be specific. In 1996, for starters.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Such as -- I mean, whom? I don't understand your question. Meaning human rights organisations from where? From Bosnia, Serbia, from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll put a few names to you now, then?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Both of you, if you cooperate a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dorothy Gallagher, a student from Louisiana?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Dorothy, as I recall, was doing data entry, if I'm not mistaken. Keeping the logs of the evidence that was being collected, if I recall well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Juereen Hoffman, a student from Arizona?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: She was a forensic pathologist from Arizona.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Clea Koff, a graduate student from Nebraska?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Molly Ryan, a student from California?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: She was a cultural anthropologist that was supporting, again, I guess data entry or something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So -- and lastly, I just mention this last one, Michael Warren, a graduate student from Florida?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Oh, Michael Warren. He's a forensic anthropologist. He was a student of late Dr. Maples.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And because it's not apparent, you know, were these people working on site or back at the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. From -- let me read the screen here. Clea worked at the site and at some point in the mortuary. Mike Warren was in the mortuary. Juereen Hoffman worked at the mortuary. Dorothy Gallagher, I think she worked at the mortuary with data entry, as well as Molly Ryan, as far as I recall. That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm being told by counsel to slow down now. So I'll heed two warnings. Let's leave those people to one side for a moment. Starting with 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because we still haven't got a clear answer whether these four or five or six individuals were ICTY staff or whether they belonged to some other organisation or human rights organisation or were they free-lance, I don't know. Perhaps you could address this, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. Baraybar, you can hear the inquiry. Can you help us as to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Based on my own recollection, and not knowing, I mean the specific arrangement or contractual status, it is my understanding that these people were employed by a physician for human rights to support the Tribunal operations. But they were not hired by ICTY itself in 1996. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, would you bear with me a minute, I just want to check your last answer on the screen. And perhaps you can help me, it would be quicker. That list of names, did you eventually agree that they were all people who worked in the mortuary or were -- or was one or more of them somebody who worked at a dig site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Primarily, as far as I recall, they all worked at the mortuary, but maybe Gallagher did some data entry at the site but I think she was at the mortuary. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, it's fine, it is 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we deal with therefore, protocol, as it were, the removal of remains from the dig site to the mortuary? Could you just please describe for us what protocols were in place relating to the removal of bodies or body parts from a dig site to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You mean the transportation or the physical removal of the remains -- I mean, from the grave site first into --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I want to know about documentation, record keeping at each end?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure. There was a -- there was a -- I recall there was a form that was filled per body that would indicate how the body was lying, I mean, any elements of clothing, whether they had ligatures or blindfolds or whatever thing you may find there. Then the body was given a number, there was one person giving the numbers, and there was the scene of crime officer, and I'm recalling, at the moment, the exhumation of Cerska, that was the first site we did. Only one person would give the numbers, as I said, otherwise you would have duplication of numbers. Then when the body has been cleaned, individualised, so to speak, I mean was ready to be lifted, that was the term that was used, a picture will be taken, or pictures would be taken of details of the body, and then you would lift the body, put into a body bag, the body bag would be placed into a refrigerated container that we had on site. Not in the site, but at the site. And then would be locked in there. And then the bodies would be taken to the mortuary, once the site has been finished. That is what I recall was -- I mean, in general terms, it was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When it arrived at the mortuary, there would have been a pathologist at the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There were many, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did every part of a body recovered go before the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. But what would happen is that, of course, the bodies would be entered, I mean a log will be done on the receiving end to see how many bags are entering, what cause, and so on. Then the bodies would be scanned by a fluoroscope, that is an X-ray machine. As a matter of fact, at the time we had a mortuary in -- in this old, bombed out factory in the place that I cannot recall at the moment. And there was an X-ray machine there, so the bodies would be primarily X-rays with the fluoroscope. Then I have a confusion; again, it has been many years. Anyway, the body would be scan the be it by a fluoroscope or X-ray machine to look for metal parts and so on, and then it would proceed to the autopsy table for examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably my fault. What I was seeking to establish, and I'm not going to make this, as it were, time specific; this could relate to the whole period of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was whether, for example, an arm bone would be taken to the pathologist or whether that would simply bypass him?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As far as I recall, nothing would bypass the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know what the pathologist would do with something in relation to which the exercise of determining cause of death was pointless?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, do remember, just to -- I mean, to give some explanation to you what you just said is the following: All the remains will go through the pathologist, no matter what, an arm, a hand, whatever. The anthropologist will be work at the table working with the forensic pathologist make the determinations that may be possible to make, and will allow or not, the pathologist to ascertain, for example, cause of death. In the case of an arm, certainly, or more than certainly, cause of death could be ascertained, unless there was a gun-shot wound through the humerus that may have, I mean, cut brachial artery and the person bled to death. But, I mean, otherwise it would be cause of death, unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the pathologist, at least in 1996 initially keep a separate record of what happened at the autopsy table from the anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That I don't know. There was a form with part -- part of which was the anthropologist's responsibility to fill in. Now, whether they were keeping a separate record, I mean a separate notebook or whatever, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, in 1996, focusing, if you want on Cerska. How many pathologists would have been working concurrently?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's a very good question. If I -- I mean I would be lying. My recollection is that there were like three tables, I think, running at the same time. I think it was a three-table mortuary we set up in that factory. So it would be three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what level of anthropologist would be at that table with each of those pathologists?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Level in terms of experience or?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, obviously Mr. Haglund couldn't be at every table.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, no, no. Haglund actually -- Haglund was not -- you know, participating in the examination of remains. He was primarily in the field. He was dealing with exhumations. Do remember that the chief pathologist at the time was a -- later Dr. Krsna [phoen], Robert Krsna. So he was the chief pathologist. There would be three pathologist and at least three or four anthropologists. They were experienced people, like Mike Warren, for example, you mentioned, and some other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You say Mike Warren was experienced but he wasn't somebody so nearly well qualified as you, was he, to make anthropological determinations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, at the time -- at the time I would not like to necessarily say that I was the most qualified person in the planet, but I have certainly much more experience regarding, I mean, case work than many other people. But there were other people that were very qualified as well. Talking about Mike Warren, he came from a laboratory in Florida that dealt with a lot of case work as well, so he was a very experienced person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So just to summarise, you are aware that in 1996 there was a pathologist sheet to be filled out in relation to any body or body part, but you are not aware whether there was an anthropologist sheet to be filled out at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. What I recall, and again it's been a long time, is there was an autopsy form that contained the pathologist's information in it and then some part to be filled by the anthropologist. Because for example your age determination, you will not kind of write on a piece of paper and give it to the pathologist. You would have filled in your information in the same form. Now, that is my recollection. Since I do not have any document in front of me, I couldn't really tell you off the top of my head, I mean 11 years after, that was the case, but that is my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In relation to this aspect of the investigation, is this -- is this an area where protocol changed and was improved after 1996?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would say that there was a lot of improvement regarding -- I mean mortuary protocol and that, yes, after 1996, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was wrong with the system in 1996 and how was it improved?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, you see, first of all the condition that we work were less than optimal. What I am telling is we were working in a bombed-out factory, a textile factory or something. Close to the former confrontation line. So there was no water, I mean the tables were improvised. I mean, a lot of the things, I mean to the hardware was quite -- wasn't really there. Electricity was a problem, again, running with generators. Things could have been done better also with better hardware and conditions of work. But one of the things we improved as well was having a much more systematic recording of bone elements and so on in -- in spread sheets to allow us to later obviously calculate all these minimal numbers and those things. We, in the years after 1996, were much more specific in our descriptions of bones that could be used, for example, the calculation of the MNI, rather than a -- saying almost complete, I don't know, femur, we would say whether we had a form where you would tick whether you have, I mean, the proximal part or the middle part or the distal part of the bone, and things of the kind. So there was much more of that. I think that came after.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got one brief-ish topic to deal with, which may just take up to a break if we're lucky, Mr. Baraybar, and you and I can have a break and everybody else can. I want to see if you can help us as to whose responsibility it was carry out various parts of the, as it were, autopsy procedure. Starting first of all with what we'll call a complete body or a nearly complete body. Whose responsibility was it to make a note of and record the parts that were missing from that body, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Primarily, if this body was skeletonised, it would be the anthropologist. If the body was fleshed, would be the pathologist in his own -- I mean autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And dealing now with a body part, whose responsibility would it be to identify what part of a body that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yet again, if you are talking about flesh remains, it would be a pathologist. If it would be very decomposed remains, it would be the anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. What about the measurement of any bone recovered or body part recovered, if indeed that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The anthropologist. I mean, whatever measurement of bone would be the responsibility of the anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The taking of any DNA samples from any body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We have actually -- or I have unintentionally I have omitted the fact that there were autopsy technicians we have forgotten about autopsy technicians. There were autopsy technicians also assisting at mortuary. At the time and throughout, I mean through the years. And I think that they were the ones, I mean, taking the sample for DNA testing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you confirm that that was routinely done in relation to every body and body part exhumed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So there is, in effect, the potential at least for a complete DNA database of -- of all the bodies and body parts exhumed in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Maybe so. Maybe so. I don't know. Were DNA samples taken, the answer is yes. Were they taken from every single bone, obviously not. I mean if you have a body part, let's assume you have a torso, you would take a sample from the arm but not from every rib and every -- the collar bone or whatever. You might just take one sample per unit. I believe you have -- the hands and feet, you will not be taking DNA sample from those, because normally DNA, to be extracted from those parts is -- is quite difficult, I mean in every possible setting. I mean-, you will always recommend to take long bones, dense bones, like femur or humerus, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was going on from 1996 throughout the whole period to 2001, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Collection of DNA, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Whose responsibility would it be to determine the sex of any body or body part that was recovered?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Fleshed, pathologist. Unfleshed, anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, the determination of the age of any body or body part, whose responsibility would that be?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If the determination of sex and age was made by the anthropologist, would that or should that have been made in the autopsy room or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In -- no, in the autopsy room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was a bad question. It's my fault, and I don't -- always quick to acknowledge that. What I'm aiming at is record keeping. If the determination of sex and age was the responsibility of the anthropologist, would it also be his responsibility to record it somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I mentioned to you, the answers yes, but as I mentioned to you, my recollection again is that you have an autopsy protocol that contains a section for the pathologist, a section for the anthropologist. Now, the -- if we try to picture the situation, you have a table with a body on it, and you have another table next to it for the anthropologist to work, otherwise everybody will be working on top of each other. And you may you know need these elements to have a look at with a closer look, or to wash them or even to boil them because they have some flesh on it and you have to go down to the bone. And you take it to the other table, do your determination, and then write in his report or dictate even to the pathologist, say, okay, age, whatever, sex, whatever, and that's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just a follow-up question from that. If it was the responsibility of the anthropologist to determine sex and age, is that something that the pathologist would simply wash his hands of and say, over to you, you deal with it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If -- regarding sex, as I said, if it is fleshed you have external genitalia, obviously the pathologist would be the one determining sex and there is no need to go further. But age, certainly, is a responsibility of the anthropologist. I mean certainly. I don't know whether the pathologist washes his hands or not. I hope he does, but the issue is that certainly that is a responsibility of the anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I probably ought to clear that up. What I meant was if -- if the determination of those factors was something that the pathologist was not going to take part in, would it be something he would not record?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: By definition, yes. I mean by definition, yes. Now, are you discussing this in the context of 1996 again or throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm really dependent on you to tell me how things changed, whether that was the position in 1996 and whether it got better in 1998 and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right, but this is not a matter of getting better or worse. It is obviously a task, a division of tasks. In other words, a pathologist is somebody who deals with a cadaver, with soft tissues, and determine cause of death based on that examinations. If you have a body part that may be totally, I mean, rotten and decomposed and beyond recognition, he or she cannot do much with that soft tissue besides saying well, it is human, it is rotting soft tissue. Now you, anthropologist, tell me something else. So clean it, get to the bone and tell me the male, female, he's young, he's old, whatever, and that's pretty much it. It has nothing to do with improvements. It's just a division of labour. The pathologist not deal with determination of sex or age on skeletal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will put this to you and we'll come back to it later. What I suggest to you is that in 1996, the pathologist -- the records that the pathologist was keeping, as to the condition of the body and what was missing from it, were found to be inadequate.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not know. I mean I -- if you can show me some example somewhere, I could give an opinion, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will later. And --

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- that in order to perform a minimum number calculation, the record had to be correlated with different records kept by the anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I've finished on that topic. I can't see what time it is. It think it's a little early, but it would be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is two minutes before our break time but we can have our break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If it is convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Mr. Haynes How much longer do you think you will be cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I'll be true to my two hours, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly not as long as we said. Perhaps 15 minutes. 10, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can afford a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a very good reminder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to move on now to the question of determining the sex of bodies and body parts. And I'd like to just clear one thing up with you to start off with. It's right, isn't it, that your calculation of the minimum number of individuals exhumed includes those for whom sex could not be determined?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's also correct, isn't it, and I'm taking the figure from the report of Dean Manning, that the number of bodies and body parts for which sex could not be determined was 253?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I have not seen the report of Dean Manning, nor do I have it in front of me, so I do not know. This 253 means bodies from when? All the bodies from 1996 to 2001 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I want to check with my own reports. I would say yes, conditional yes, because I have not seen the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. But in round terms, about 10 per cent of the minimum number of individuals, or sorry the minimal minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That would be, yes, I think it's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
