utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that the best way, in fact the only certain way of determining the sex of any individual, is to identify them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You would not agree that if you can establish the identity of the person and that person is a man or a woman, that is in the best way of determining sex?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You are talking about personal identity, meaning to name one person?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. For example if you had a -- if you took a DNA sample and you could relate it to somebody from whom you had a DNA sample, and you could establish that that person was a man or a woman. That's the best way of ascertaining the sex of an individual, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, if you -- sequencing the Y chromosome, of course, you will know whether this person is a male or not, but, I mean, I would not agree. I mean there are other ways to determine sex because sex is part of the identity of a person. So let's look at the problem in reverse. We find a set of skeletal remains. In other context, let's forget for a moment this specific case, you don't know who this person is. You don't have a clue as to who this person may be. So you have to come up with some elements as to try to draw a biological profile that could be compared with a list of persons missing in that jurisdiction. So you have to be able to say that this person is male or female based on some basic elements, otherwise imagine in all the pre-DNA times meaning 20 years ago, how people would do determine it, sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Baraybar, nothing we are talking about is in pre-DNA times. You were taking DNA samples from everybody throughout the whole of the investigation, according to your evidence. It's a simple proposition. If you don't agree with it, I'll move on. But isn't it right that if you can actually identify -- you can actually establish the identity of somebody, that's the only fool-proof way of determining their sex?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I do not agree, I'm afraid, with you. Certainly I can provide you other arguments, but no, I do not agree with you. I mean if you want, I can expand on it, otherwise we'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, it's really not necessary. We'll disagree on that. As you've told us a number of the bodies and body parts that were the subject of autopsies were visibly one sex or another, because they had external genitalia or the like, and so that would be the next best way of establishing the sex of a body or body part. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after that you have to rely on certain features of the body or body parts to determine sex. Would you agree that the next most reliable test as to what the sex of a body or body part is, is analysis of the pelvis girdle?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after that, analysis of the skull?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us that you have in front of you some scientific literature. I imagine that that literature includes the article in Science Direct that you provided to the Prosecution last week?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Djuric et al, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you accept their findings that analysis of the skull to determine sex is only of -- ever 70 per cent successful?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In the sample they worked with, yes. Remember, I mean this article is based on a very specific sample. So based on the findings on that sample, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after analysis of the skull, as it were, the last resort for determining sex is analysis of long bones, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you agree that that is a less certain system of analysis than even analysis of the skull?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. It is in an order of priorities, would be pelvis, skull, long bones. And obviously the accuracy will decrease as you go along that path, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the sex determinations that you have knowledge of, which of those techniques would you say was most commonly used?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, depending on what did you have. If you have, I mean, a complete body, you would go first for the pelvis. And then you would have a look at the skull as well. Long bones would not be necessary for that matter. If you had a body part that did not have the pelvis but only long bones, you would be pretty much left with whatever you could do with the long bones. So you could measure certain parts of those bones and apply certain formula that exist or simply you couldn't. And if you couldn't, you would be -- this individual would be classified as undetermined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to get accused of asking the same question twice, but what I was really from in the question I asked was whether you could say now whether it was long bone analysis that was most commonly used in the determination of sex or any other of those tests that I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. As I said, and I think I have written that in my reports, the analysis of sex was carried out in the fashion I told you. Pelvis first, skull after, and long bones later. If you refer to long bone analysis, that's a specific testifying that I used in some of my reports or in some of the forms that are a way of scoring the presence of a specific part of a long bone to facilitate the calculation of the MNI. So the answer is still the same. We have used the pelvis first, skull later, and long bones as a last resort, if there is nothing else to determine sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So -- and I'm taking this particular bone from your report, if the only body part you had was a left proximal femur, how would you determine the sex of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most likely you would use the maximum diameter of the femural head. Back in early 1900s if I am not mistaken, Pearson, if that is correct as well, if my recollection doesn't fail, established a set of measurements of the femural head where there is a cut-off point for males and females and that was based on a Caucasian for a white, European population sample. So that would be one of the ways that you would use. But certainly we would not have been, let's say, relying 100 per cent on this. For example, let's assume the following. The cut-off point is 42 millimetres or up to 42 millimetres for females and then from 47 millimetres up are males. So what happened between 42 and 47? Obviously you would not say somebody with a 45-millimetre measurement, you could not say, well, could be a male. I mean, obviously this person would be classified as undetermined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that in minute, but I want to now move on to the question of age determination. And I'm going to put the same proposition to you and see whether you agree with it. The best and only fool-proof method of age determination is actual identification of the individual?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, it is a very tricky question, primarily because we are defining two different types of data. Let me explain. Identity will give you chronological age determination, right, because you have somebody's name at the end of the day, full identity of the this person, date of birth, et cetera, that will give you chronological age. When we deal with bones we are talking about biological age, so those two things cannot be compared. A bone will not give you a chronological age; by definition, it is impossible. You would not be able to say this person is 25 years and seven months to his or her birthday. That is simply impossible. So to clarify your or answer your question, it would be yes, personal identity through DNA or whatever would give you chronological age determination. However, anthropology work on bones will give you biological age determination. That is not comparable. Because in anthropology you are creating a range where you would fit this person. So, for example, you have an individual between 20 and 30, doesn't really matter whether the person is 21 and a half or 25. The issue is that this person has to be -- has to fall within this age, this biological age interval. So there are two different things. I don't know whether that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you. Now, the techniques that you used for age determine nation are set out at page 6 of your minimum number of individuals report, which is, if it can be put on to e-court, P02477 at page 6. Sorry, we have to wait for other people to see it on the screen, Mr. Baraybar; that's why I'm pausing. This is for everybody's else's benefit, Mr. Baraybar, not for you. The relevant paragraph is the English is the one beginning "age" at the top of the page. I am guessing the relevant paragraph in the B/C/S is the one beginning "Pol" towards the bottom of the page. No. No, it's not. That's sex. It must be up a little bit. Maybe back a page in the -- no, no. It must be back a page in the B/C/S, please. No, you've gone forward. I think you really need to go backwards. Thank you. "Storosna Do" [phoen] at the very bottom. In the B/C/S we're going to have to give people a chance to read that paragraph and then go over to the next page. According to that you used two techniques for determining age in bodies or body parts exhumed by you. Changes in the sternal end of the fourth rib, and analysis of changes in the pubic symphysis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: For the adults, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And for children, epiphyseal union in children. You didn't use any other tests to determine age?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. Primarily what is listed in this report, we will have used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And again, just referring you to the article you kindly provided us with, the Djunic and other article, their findings would indicate that analysis of age by the two techniques used by you had a 67 per cent accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, if you read carefully the article I presented to you, primarily the accuracy is referred to the precision that they used in determining the age intervals. And what they said is that when they use for example a plus, minus 2.5 years, of a specific estimate, they were having a lower, I mean an accuracy that when using a broader range. So that is one thing. The second thing is that the application of a specific technique to a specific population will also reflect the age distribution of the population that you are working with. If I may explain yet a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but I am going to come on to that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you make a wider bracket then you are more likely to be accurate, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but whilst in about 10 per cent of the cases that form the minimum number of individuals, it was not possible to determine sex. There is no single body or body part in which a determination of age was not made. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this I would welcome your explanation on. How do you determine the age of, for example, the left proximal femur, if you don't know what sex it is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, obviously the -- in order to determine age you have to go through sex first. Because you have different rates of maturation between the sexes. I mean females, they age skeletally faster than males. That is correct. Having said that we have to take into consideration, what does it mean in terms of years or time. In other words, if I have a proximal femur, as you said, and I do not know what sex it is, okay, I may be saying, okay, this person is an adult. But that adult term, meaning that everything is fused, there is nothing unfused, just -- is as applicable to a male as it is applicable to a female. I cannot differentiate whether -- I mean, this person was 25, 26, or maybe 24 and a half, I cannot. So it is applicable to both. Now, as per the remains of a younger -- younger people, in which again you do not have the sex, that's why we have created a broader bracket that could actually be applicable so much for a male as to a female. As you have seen, the brackets are quite broad, so you know they can tolerate, so to speak, a mixture of sexes, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let me take this step by step. You accept that an age determination was made in relation to every body or body part you recovered, every body or body part that forms the minimum number of individuals. Let me take it step by step. How do you determine, given the criteria you used, the age of a left proximal femur? Because that's -- you haven't got a pubic symphysis, and you haven't got a sternal end to the fourth rib. So how do you determine the age of that bone?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, in a very simple manner. You have only two options with the left proximal femur. Whether that person is a mature or juvenile person, whether you're going to see that the pieces are unfused, or in the process of fusion, or whether anything is fused. If everything is fused you know this person is an adult. An adult could be over 25, over 23 and a half. Yes, it is possible, but you don't know. Therefore, it is 25 plus. The reason why we have created such a, I mean, broad interval of, say, 25 to infinite, so to speak, is because of that reason. Exactly that reason. Now, there is another element I have to say. Regarding the body parts, we have estimated in relative interpretation age of body parts whenever possible. For example, you have a hand. Okay. You have a hand. In which everything is fused, there is nothing unfused or in the profess of fusion, so is the hand of somebody, male or female, that has stopped, let's say, maturing or growing, to put it in a more popular term. Therefore, this person is an adult. Whether it is a male or female is another matter. And that is something you cannot really say base on that hand. Of course you could, if you take every bone and apply some formula and maybe you come up with some sex estimation for that hand. But that hand would be going to be the 25 plus category on one hand, and on the other hand, would not be used for your MNI. I mean, your MNI would not be using hands, I mean, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but your MNI uses quite a lot of bones in relation to which you couldn't determine sex or age with any accuracy, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It does. Again up to a certain extent. I don't know whether I have made myself clear with this. Accuracy is dependent on what you have in order to determine an age range. So we agree with that. Now, whenever you have something that has stopped fusing, growing, maturing or whatever we want to call it, okay, these specific parts will go on to the 25 plus category. Then you tell me, the 25 plus category, you cannot do better than that. Of course I can't. But what I can do better, I mean, we can look at some of the other reports of the previous years, is that we have broken down in some cases the 25 plus category based on more diagnostic elements such as the pubic symphysis. So, for example, in one of the reports that I have here from -- let me see. For example, the report of 1999, anthropological examination of human remains from Eastern Bosnia, 1998, there we have a breakdown by mean ages of all the parts that contain pubic symphysis. And that is part of the 25 plus interval. But certainly as you will say, we did not have pubic symphysis in every case, and in some cases we are only using, let's say, proximal left femur. Having said that let me just finalise my thought here, that when I say that we use the proximal left femur for the MNI, it does not mean that we had only broken, isolated, left proximal femur. That femur could be part of a pelvis, that could be part of a complete body. But in order to homogenise your calculations, we were counting in the body, the proximal left femur. It is very important. I mean, these are -- by no means I'm saying we have only a collection of left proximal femur and there was nothing else. That is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So to summarise, would you accept that necessarily age determination in bodies or certainly body parts where you could not determine sex, is a less exact, an even less exact science?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I wouldn't say a less exact science is a less accurate procedure. But, I mean, all the procedures we are dealing with are scientific procedures, I mean, so therefore, yes, it is a less accurate procedure but is not -- nothing do with science. No, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. And secondly, where you did not have either a sternal end of the fourth rib or a pubic symphysis, it seems to me, from what you're saying, you just put that body part in the 25 plus category. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If there was nothing -- if we had any kind of bone other than the one you just listed for the adults, very clear for the adults, and there is nothing in the process of fusion, nothing maturing, nothing that would indicate a person that was in the process of, let's say, quote unquote, "growing," this person would be put in the 25 plus category? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, lastly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If counsel could make pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Lastly on this topic, was there an element of professional input from the anthropologist in some cases to age determination?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you a passage from a report, please. It's P0611 at page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get whose report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is Bill Haglund's report. And I think it's the first one. The Cerska report. I say, It's page 41, not 31.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Does counsel have the page number in the B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we try with 41 and see where we go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It is the same page, and it's paragraph C. The English has gone down too far now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund used rather more features of the body to determine age than you did, as we can see from the first paragraph. But he says in the middle of the second paragraph under age estimation, "The final mean age estimation is based on a combination of the aforementioned factors plus the anthropologist's own judgement. The minimum and max number age are equal to minus one and plus one, the standard error, respectively. The final age -- range given is the anthropologist's opinion of the individual's biological age and does not exclude the possibility that the true calendar age is outside the range given." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, most definitely. But just to clarify your point, he did not use more standards than we did. As a matter of fact, the medial clavicle that is referred there, is part of the McClelland and Stewart [phoen] standards, and also it is an epiphysis. I mean, they are mentioning the medial epiphysis of the clavicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to. And presumably that -- what Mr. Haglund is saying there is that if, for example, you have a pubic symphysis which indicates that a body is, let's say for the sake of argument, 14 years of age, but the bones you have indicate that he's 1.9 metres tall, the anthropologist might override, as it were, the finding of the pubic symphysis. Is that -- is that something that would have occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Hold on. I'm reading your question again because I did not really --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's partly my fault. I'm getting too fast again, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, it's not the pace, actually. I did not under -- follow your thought. Could you maybe rephrase your question, because I mean I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. Were there occasions when the anthropologist's opinion would take precedence over the findings as determined by the sternal end of the fourth rib or the pubic symphysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, no. Because I mean the anthropologist would be taking all these elements into consideration. If we go back to the text that I'm reading here, it's a very common sensical statement. It has nothing to do with Haglund or anybody else. It is a very common anthropological practice. In other words, you have a standard, okay. The standard tells you phase one means A, B, and C. Okay. And you have been trained to understand what those standards actually mean, and when you observe a pube, you can say, okay, this is phase whatever. Then you look at a rib and combine all these elements. Now, obviously you have certain parameters to establish an interval, an age interval. But, as I said, the age interval, the brackets, in order to be accurate, they have to contain the real age, meaning the chronological age of the individual that you do not have within it. Okay. So as pointed out in this paper by Djuric et al, whenever you have a range that is more precise, you are losing accuracy. Because you can say that this person is between 14 and 16, but maybe the person is 17. And because you had only a plus minus of one, right, you have left this person outside. You have excluded this person. So that is just to comment, I mean, the text you show me. And I don't know whether I have answered your question, but it is still -- I mean -- I don't know whether I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on because we're going to come back to this in another context. I'm going to now move on the subject that you were anxious to talk about earlier. Changes in the pubic symphysis to an extent vary according to racial or regional origin, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, no. As a matter of fact, it is slightly more complicated than that. Populations proceed -- variation is a combination of a lot of factors that can go from nutrition to ancestry to sex to a number of things, certainly. So, yes, what I would say, it is safer to say that either there is variation across populations regarding the way that certain parameters, I mean change, get -- I mean modify age, if you wish, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And prior to 1999 the basis for comparison in relation to change in the pubic symphysis was the Suchey Brooks standard, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. And still is, as a matter of fact. As a technique, it still is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But that was based on, you will correct me if I'm wrong, a survey of North American subjects, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is a sample assembled at Los Angeles medical examiner's office. So it is -- it is a -- yes, a contemporary North American multi-racial sample. We will call it this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when you took charge of exhumations in 1999, you immediately adopted a different standard for comparison, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What we did is we used the same standard, meaning -- the Suchey Brooks technique, is a technique that -- that is made of phases, so those phases, the standard itself has not changed. In 1999 what became available was a different distribution of ages per phase based on a more specific population for the Balkans, specifically from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that, in your view, a better source of comparison for age determination in the pubic symphysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Definitely at the time was the newest or more relevant, if you wish, source available. Meaning it is very possible that if we were -- if we kept, let's say, using Suchey brooks as per the North American standards, we would be underestimating or overestimating the age of people we were observing. However, having by then available a study more relevant to the region, it would make sense to adopt it. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were any of the age determinations prior to 1999 reevaluated after 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not think so, no. Just in the cases -- the most important thing to remember is the following, just for clarity: Each phase remains what it is. In other words, if I observe let's in 1996 a pube that was phase two, my observation at phase two will remain the same. That doesn't change. But if phase two comes from -- I'm just making it up. Whether some 20 to 30 years, maybe according to this new population study, a phase two would mean, let's say, 40 to 50. So what we change would be the construction of the age interval and not the observation I made. So whenever it was possible, and again I am recalling here, we, or I, for that matter, recalculated that. But I think that this has been recalculated only from 1999 onwards, not for the data before. I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because I haven't got my LiveNote on screen at the moment, whether you've given the name of the 1999 report. That was the Simmons report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Simmons, yes. It is in the bibliography, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I just wanted it on the record. Was the Simmons report, in your view, perfectly adequate as a benchmark for determining the age of the people you exhumed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It's not the benchmark of anything. As I told you, again, it was the most appropriate population sample available at the time. We could engage into a discussion as to whether the statistics used for example were appropriate or not and that's really another matter. What I would say is that at the time this report, this paper, that was submitted to -- in a forensic meeting, was the closest in a way to what would have been needed. Maybe earlier on, you know. But I mean of course these kind of things are not things you do from one day to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just two more things on this particular topic. Would it be your evidence therefore that the age assessments based on Suchey Brooks prior to 1999 have an additional element of inaccuracy?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is highly likely that construction of the age intervals, based on a population sample that was not from the Balkans, that as an inherent error that it may be an error, but a systematic error because it has been used throughout. So at least you know it has an error but a systematic error. Now, what do I mean by this? As I told you, since the technique is the same, but the vales, if you wish, or trait you are observing, the face, are different, what you would be doing is you would be systematically underaging or overaging people. But systematically. Okay? So this is extremely important. This is not a -- a -- half this other thing that changes, I mean, let's say from year to year. As long as you know that -- as long as you are consistent with your source of error, in a way, you know that the error exists. And answer is yes, there is a tendency either to over or underestimate age of people. By how much, or, you know, by how much? Well, the data we have at the moment is that according to -- I mean Simmons and some other studies done on the matter on samples from the Balkans is -- in the Balkans compared to American standards, people may be -- seem to be the older, you know, for the same phases. So a phase two, again, just making it up, a phase two in the U.S. sample may be, let's say, 20 to 30, while in the Balkans it would be 25 to 35, or 30 to 40, something of the kind. I'm just giving this to illustrate what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm glad you used the word systematic, because, of course, it would be systematic if you carried on using the same test. But you changed it in 1999, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We did not, I already told you twice, change the test. What we changed were the values for the same tests. The test has not changed. Suchey Brooks is Suchey Brooks. It's a six-phase system by which you observe a number of characteristics per phase on the pubic symphysis. What changes is what phase one means in the Balkans and what phase one means in the U.S. That is what changes. So it is the same technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that there has been further research. Is that on a Balkan-specific population that is post-1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is, yes. But it is not post- -- what is post-1999, the sample or the research?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The research.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yeah, the research, yes. As a matter of fact, there is a series of -- of papers that are under peer review at the moment in the Journal of Forensic Sciences. It is 10 papers that are reformulating the Suchey Brooks phases and issuing and loss of phases for the ribs in a Balkan population sample. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is any of this research, research you have carried out yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I could say yes, I am part of that research as a whole, yes, but I have not individually carried out the research of all those things, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does the research involve the analysis of some of the bones and body parts we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is it research that you have initiated?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is research that I have, let's say, devised, if you -- if you wish to use that term, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Exactly the type of discussion we are having today. Meaning the relevancy of age standards for the population we are working. In other words, whenever you work in a specific place in a country in a region, you will use whatever you have at hand. But you know that the best thing you can have is to have standards that reflect that specific population you are working with. So we knew that all we had at the time, and for years, was what was there, you know, set up in North America, whatever. But there was something needed actually for the types of populations we were working with. So these new standards hopefully will assist in the age determination of, I mean, thousands of our victims of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would no doubt have assisted you, had you had it available in 1999 to 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to age groupings now. I think I've understood you correctly that no attempt was made by you or your team, and I am dealing specifically with the sites that were in control of, to place precise ages on body parts as opposed to placing them in an age group, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Every body or body part was placed in an age range. Not even a complete body was placed in a specific pin-point age. That doesn't work. I mean, as I said before, you will not be able, when determining biological age, to say this person is 24 and a half. You can't. So everything, body parts and bodies will be placed in age ranges. The difference is that when you have obviously as I said a hand for example, and everything is fused, you will say, well, it is an adult and will be no even age attached to it, it will be, say, 25 plus. That is a statement, just to say it's an adult, I cannot say more about it. Obviously in another individual, you would say, this person is between 18 and 24 based on A, B, C, D, but this person still will be fit into an age interval later because, see, we're talking about hundreds of thousands of cases. I mean you have to -- you have to present them in some fashion. I mean, you cannot really list every single individual, you would go through years doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The age groupings used by you were rather different from those used by Mr. Haglund, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Do you have anything on Haglund's age groupings? I mean on the top of my head, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we can come to it later but I will put it to you now. If you don't know the answer, I will wait until we can get it up on screen.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that they were and that in itself is unsystematic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I will keep my question [sic] when you show me the paper, and then I can reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I perfectly respect you for that.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The page that we still have on screen under age estimation, Mr. Haglund suggests that each age grouping, the minimum and maximum age are equal to minus one, plus one, standard error. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Where are you looking sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph under age estimation.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, yeah. I mean we can go on to -- we can elaborate this a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you agree that the age groupings that you used are subject to a minus one, plus one standard error at the minimum and maximum age parameters?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I would say I would be using two. I would be using, I mean, two standard deviations that more or less tends to be placing your result at the 95 per cent confidence interval, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I mean, I want to be clear about this. Are you saying that your age groupings are subject to a minus two/plus two error?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. We have much more of a -- generous intervals, if you wish, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to -- there to be any mystery about this, perhaps you better put P0477 at page 8 into e-court, please. And the ERN number at the top of the page is 0348-9051. And it certainly shouldn't be a newspaper article. The Prosecution Exhibit Number is 0477, or 00477 -- oh, I'm sorry. Let me just check that. Sorry. It's 02477. My mistake. There really is no point in having the translated version of this on the screen. We might as well just have one, it's only a list. Can we go forward one page? That's actually page 7, I want page 8. It's probably a page ahead in B/C/S, which is what we've got on screen. Mr. Baraybar, it's probably easier for you just to turn to page 8 of your report so you can see it in front of you. I dare say you already have. Now, here we see the age groupings that you employed and there are four of them, aren't there? There is eight to 12, 13 to 17, 15 to 24, and over 25?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, in your last answer, are you conceding that the plus or minus error level should mean that those groups read six to 14, 11 to 19, 13 to 26, and 23 plus?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. Because I could put it to you as well that they could read 10 plus minus two, or 15 plus minus two, et cetera. The point -- we have to be very careful with the issue of confidence intervals and standard deviation. Remember that if I -- I have given you an answer regarding some deviation and using two standard deviations to be generous, in terms of the interval I am making. I am not, however, calculating statistically a standard deviation or a mean for a specific estimate I am -- I am doing. Okay. So the answer I have given you is based first on Haglund's report of the plus/minus one side deviation, whatever. But I mean, that is a way to put it. I mean, I would not really concentrate on standard deviation as such because we are not calculating standard deviations per estimate per case. So it's just a -- a type of warning because then we're talking about completely two different things. I don't know if that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's not. I don't understand what you're saying. I thought in answer to the question earlier, did you agree with Mr. Haglund's assertion that the age groupings were subject to a plus one/minus one error, at the minimum and maximum age, I thought you said no, it should be two.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What I said is the following: In statistical terms, when you use two standard deviations as a norm, you are approaching the 95 per cent confidence interval. That is the first statement. The second statement is the following: If Haglund is saying that he estimating one standard deviation above and on top of a mean, my interpretation of that is it -- it is more a wording because I do not see how, okay, you will be able to estimate a standard deviation for an estimate based on a range. Now, what I have said is that we were using the equivalent, there would be two standard deviations. What I am trying to say is, we have created, and I say that, more generous ranges to be as inclusive as possible, regarding the ages that have been derived from the standards we are using. But we are not doing a mathematical calculation per case to say, okay, you know, it is 17.5 plus minus 2.8, that is the standard deviation because there is no way to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to come back to you on that. You are suggesting, are you, that you have created more generous ranges than Dr. Bill Haglund?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We might have to come back to that in minute.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But anyway, I want to come back to something else, and to that end I would like to -- you to have a look at page 6 of your report. It's the same exhibit number we just need to go back two pages in the English and in the B/C/S. And I want to -- I want you to concentrate really on the last paragraph under the heading "age." Now, in pretty much the last sentence of that section you say, "Remains of individuals falling in this category," that's the eight to 12 year-old category, "are represented primarily by long bones of small size with unfused epiphysis." I can't say that word. "There is bound to be some overlap between those individuals at the end of the first and fourth and the beginning of the second." You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that another way of saying that we cannot be sure that any body part assessed is being -- eight to 12 years of age is not properly placed in the next group up?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct. But let me interject one thing here, because I understand -- I think I understand where the confusion may lie. There are two different things, we are talking about two different things here. The age intervals that I have used for reporting, okay, are one thing. The age interval given to a specific individual in the autopsy report is something else. In other words, I am not aging everybody as being eight to 12 or 13 to whatever. I mean, it is not working that way. Having the thousands of cases with specific ages, could be, let's say, 17 to -- to 21, you know, where will you put it? Okay you could put it in the 15 to 24. That there would be a chance that this individual was actually 16 and a half, and they should be placed in the other category. That is totally possible. And primarily, when you talk about young people, and even if you have only a long bone or whatever, that is completely possible. It is definitely possible. But do remember, you can use certain standards to calculate, for example, the length of a bone, that it have everything fused. Okay, let's say you have the femur and everything unfused, so you know that the epiphyseal is unfused and [indiscernible] fused, and you can measure that bone and get an idea, this person may be between so and so years. Now that -- that specific individual have a growing disorder, and was really older but looked younger, yes, it is possible. It is completely possible. So to answer your question, yes. I mean, totally. I mean, I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to be clear about where I'm going with this. We are in a criminal court here, and I'm really asking you whether we can be sure of the ages placed upon some of these bones and you seem to agree with me that if a bone is aged between eight and 12 we cannot be sure that it is not properly placed in the next category up. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, but -- just like leave it for the record again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has explained it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, even allowing for whatever your evidence is about, as it were, margins for error at the edges of the groupings, the next two groups up, that's 13 to 17 and 15 to 24, have an express overlap, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so it must necessarily be the case that we can never be sure as to which of those two groups any particular body or body part falls into. And in particular I'm think of body parts.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. So the safest way to put it would be that this body or body parts will fall into the interval 13 to 24, because you cannot differentiate whether they belong to the first segment or the second segment or some interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But, of course, you haven't got a 13 to 24 grouping, you've got a 13 to 17, and a 15 to 24?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct. But if we go back to -- and I'm going look for one -- all the reports here. Remember that the age intervals were constructed to fit data into them. Doesn't mean that this interval we have constructed to age people. Okay? People were aged with the techniques we have already mentioned and that. Now, if we have a look at for example one of the reports of 8th of September -- 8th of December, 1999, called Report of Anthropologist's Examination of Human Remains from Eastern Bosnia in 1999, you will see there that we have a category of 13 to 24. So you would ask me now most likely why I have changed it then later. Because later we were trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were the one who used the word "systematic." Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If you would, then, if I may just answer the question straight out. Much later, meaning this last report from 2004, we have to pull out all the information we had at the time. 1996 included with all the differences we have seen and everything. So in order to try to fit all that into some sensical order, we have created those categories. But, I mean, I'm the first one to admit that, yes, there is overlap. So -- but not because there is overlap, it changes -- I mean, the -- the substance of it, is what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to finish this by just asking you whether you would similarly concede that there is the possibility for substantial overlap between the 15 to 24 group and the 25 plus group?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not agree. Because the hallmark of the 25 plus is exactly to be an adult. To have nothing in fusion, to have nothing in between, nothing in sort of growing terms or whatever. It's just a complete, fully ossified, fused bone. There's nothing young about it, if you wish. I'm talking in very anthropological jargon at the moment, but I mean, in forensic anthropology or physical anthropology, you can actually very easily see if one person is, we say, is on the young end or on the adult end. Now, this person could be 25 or could be 35. I mean, that's another matter. I mean, many of the people in this courtroom, I mean, could look younger or older. Skeletally, maybe we are all the same. And it is extremely possible. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on to the minimum number of individuals, please. And I only want to deal, to start off with, the exhumations you were in charge of. I've asked this question in a different form, but you should be more able to answer it this time, which is: How many complete bodies did you exhume?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, we can go back to my reports. I would not be able to tell you off the top of my head, certainly, how many there were, but if you allow me for a moment, I will look for the reports from 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Please feel free.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. There are several. I have a report here from 23rd of November, 2001. Report and excavation of Glogova 2, from 1999 to 2001. Well, in this report when we referred to Glogova 2, I say -- I use a minimum number of individuals, so I do not use the term complete bodies. On -- when use GL03, we said that we have found the remains of at least 11 bodies, and, if I recall well, these were the bodies left behind after robbing of the grave. We move to GL05. We have 73 complete or almost complete bodies and a number of body parts. GL07 was also robbed. We have 20 complete or almost complete bodies and a number of body parts and so on. I mean, I could add them up if you wish, but, I mean, it would take me a bit of a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There may be a way we can deal with that without wasting your time.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But thus far, on my reckoning, you've got to 104?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I have not added them up now, but I mean I would take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. Now, what records do you have of which parts, if any, were missing from those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any I record with me here, but those who carried out the anthropology examination at the mortuary would have complete forms indicating a skeletal inventory form. We have very complete skeletal inventory form where you count the finger bones or the feet of the hand to say how many are present and missing and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What correlation was ever made between bones missing from bodies at sites you exhumed with bones used to calculate the minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Correlate such as what? Whether one hand found in one site will fit the arm of somebody else in another grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the -- that's the net effect of it, but yes. What records were kept of what bones were missing, did it -- did it particularise or -- whether they were left or right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Of course. Inventory forms are actually inventory. So you would pin-point what bone is it, what part of the bone is missing, if it's left or right, yes, you would.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that information conveyed to any anthropologist who was carrying out a minimum-number-of-individuals calculation?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The anthropologist in question calculating the MNI would be me, and the answer would be yes, otherwise I would not have been able to calculate the MNI. I mean, that is actually the data I would use to calculate the MNI. This very long and boring Excel spread sheets with the information regarding what part of the bone is missing, what is the bone most -- let's say, popular in that assemblage to be used for counting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the pathologist's report specify whether the bones missing from complete bodies were left or right bones?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The pathologist. I do not know, to tell the truth. Maybe, maybe they did. But, I mean, it's like I would not -- and please do not take this in any -- any bad way, but I would not be, let's say, using the pathologist's report to calculate the MNI. I would be using anthropologist's information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to, please, go back to P02477. And we'll have a look at page 7, please. And I want to ask you what is the supporting material, what is the evidence that underlies the figures that we see in the column headed, "MNI"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The individual -- I mean the logs, I would call them logs of data collected at the mortuary. So this spread sheets, I was being mentioning, meaning the same information the way that was on paper that has been put into Excel spread sheets with the data. On -- sorry, on type of bone, left or right, proximal, distal, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in relation to the sites you didn't excavate, that is also true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: This represents every single piece of information we could get hold of, yes. Whether I dug it or not, that is what it represents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I want to press you on this. In relation to sites you didn't personally excavate or take charge of the excavation of -- the figures in there comes from -- not from other people's reports but from information you derived from the mortuary. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever was done in the mortuary, according to the -- I mean, ways and protocols we have already established is reflected in this -- in this work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've had this opportunity once, but just so we can focus on it, I'd like you just briefly, in a sentence or two, to describe the basis for the calculation of the minimum number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I will try my best. It would not be two phrases but slightly longer. But I will try my best. The minimal number of individuals, as definition is a calculation to state how many -- at least how many people would have been necessary to account for the bones we have in an assemblage. Assemblage meaning the grave, in this case. If a body has 206 bones and we have five people, these articulated in each bone possibly, we have, like, 1.030 bones. You need to find out from all these 1.030 bones, how many people you have in there. The way to calculate the MNI would be to count. And the simplest way to calculate the MNI, it's more complicated than that, but I will just give you the easy answer and we can go later with your questions on to more sophisticated aspects of it, would be to count one of a pair or a unique bone. For example, everybody has only one first cervical vertebrae, the atlas, right, so if you count five at least, you have at least five people. Or one bone of a pair. If you have a right and left femur, you will take the right femur only. Not the right and the left, but only the right. Now, when bones are fragmented, you have to even be more specific. If you take, for example, long bones you have to take only that specific portion of the bone that cannot be repeated anywhere else. So for the proximal left femur, fine. But there are other additions to this, as I already said at the beginning. During my examination, as a matter of fact. And things to do with age. You may have in the same assemblage bones that reflect something different than what has been established in your calculation. So you have been counting this femur, I told you this left proximal femur, but then you find a piece of -- I don't know, a tooth, okay, a tooth, that is a second molar that has no roots, and you know that this person may be somebody about 12 years of age, more or less, you know, give and take a couple of years. But that person is never presented by age by the femur you just counted. It happened to be adult. So you have to add that tooth as another individual to your calculation. Although you count in there femur and a tooth and you tell me, well, that's not the same thing. But you know that the femur do not represent the individual of the tooth. Because all your femur are as a matter of fact fused and adult in the way I have already explained. We can go on with our levels of complexity, if you wish, but, I mean, you tell me if you are satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no. But critical to this technique is age determination, isn't it? It's -- the determination of age is the way you say you can rule out the possibility of double accounting?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely. Most definitely. But what I have given you are extreme examples of this. So you may indeed, I know -- I mean, I know what you're trying to tell me; sure, yeah, of course. I mean, age determination is paramount to this. But by the same token, the -- the MNI is very -- is calculated on very clear, again, parameters. So what I told you is that you would be adding individuals only in cases in which it is so obvious that these people are never presented in your assemblage. So morphologically obvious, so obvious to anybody. It is not, you know, it has to go through your eyes. It's not something that is not only on paper, it's something that -- for example, let's just take a very particular example. I have an assemblage, a grave and I have in the grave 25 femur, whatever. According to the description, all these femur are indeed, you know, fused, adult individuals, fine. And then I find an arm bone, a humerus that happened to be a -- 15 millimetres long. I do know then 100 per cent that is it is highly unlikely that somebody would have an adult leg and then the arm of a child. I mean, it is simply impossible. That is impossible. Therefore that would be the only way to add that person there. But I would not be adding people so freely because the way I did my -- or this bone here is, like, young-looking, whatever, let's just it up as another individual, because then I will be overestimating. It will not be a minimal number. It will be a -- I don't know what name we can come up with. I mean, it would not be a minimal number. Minimal number is a very conservative estimate. It is very conservative. You -- it is an underestimate, not an overestimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go over to page 8, please, on this same document? Now, you've already dealt with this. You told us we can't be sure that anybody in the eight to 12 group is not properly placed in the 13 to 17 group. So looking at that chart, if we go down to Cancari Road 3, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It would be your evidence, wouldn't it, that the two that we see in that column we cannot be sure ought not to be body parts that were properly classified as 13 to 17?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The way I would phrase it is the following: Is it possible that the individuals in the eight to 12 category could actually be part of the 13 to 17 category? Yes, it is possible. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we go up to, say, the top entry. Cerska. And we'll look at the next box. And I'm not going to go through the whole thing but let's have a look. We've got nine people there aged 13 to 17. It's equally possible, isn't it, that all nine of those are aged 15 -- are aged 14 and 15?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, you -- in this example, I think it is reverse because in Cerska and like in all the other sites they were complete bodies. So in Cerska we were able to do an age determination with much more informed than in -- in Cancari Road which is a secondary site with body parts and all the rest of it. So I would say in the specific case of Cerska, it is more unlikely that that would be the case. Now, is it possible? Yeah. Everything is possible. 50/50, you know. Possibility is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So again your evidence would be that we can't be sure that those placed in the 13 to 17 category were not properly placed in the 15 to 24 category?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Regarding Cerska?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll pick another site if we're going to get site specific.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Please do so, because. I mean, it is a site-specific matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to Cancari Road 12.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, as I told you already for that site, it's a secondary site, therefore the answer is yes. I mean, the more fragmentary the remains are, you have the possibility, yes, that the one individual from the eight to 12 could be placed in the 13 to 17 or the 13 to 17 to the 15 to 24. Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But Mr. Baraybar, there is an express overlap between those. You've made a group of 15 to 24 which includes 15, 16, and 17-year-olds, all of whom appear in the lower group. You must admit of the possibility that in every single site there is possibility of double accounting of these body parts?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not double accounting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's my phrase.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right, but it is -- it is incorrect. I am correcting it. It is a matter of accounting. Accounting is counting things. That -- this is attribution, this is distribution. It is whether this individual is on this age range or the other. It is possible? Yes, it is possible. But why the overlap? Because we are talking about biological age and it doesn't exist, for example, a bone that fuses with the other at age 16.5 in every possible individual. Of course not. That doesn't happen. So the overlap is express. So in answer to your question, yes, there is bound to be overlap. Yes, there is bound to be swapping, let's say, between categories, you know. This is primarily a way to express a distribution. But what is something completely different is the issue of accounting. I mean, accounting is not the distribution of individuals with a given age range. For example, I give you a list of people. What age range is it? Okay. Show me in the best possible way you can. You will come up with a graph, with a column chart, with a -- whatever. But the accounting is another matter. We can go on the accounting. And I understand that your fear is that because the age tends to be overlapped, you may be counting twice bones. No. That is not the case. Because counting bones is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm simply sorry, I don't understand that. How, if you can't be sure whether one bone is not the bone of a 16-year-old, can you be sure that that bone is not placed -- is not -- as it were, not married up with another bone in another category? You simply can't be sure of that, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you. Because the fact of the matter is the following: You use first the most common bone you have in the assemblage, okay. That is your first -- I mean assumption. You're going to take the left proximal femur, fine. Within the left proximal femur, the easiest group you will get to, say, rid of would be the adults, okay, the non-fusing, non-growing, nothing. I mean, you know these people are full adult bones with nothing missing. That is what you have. So you've got 25 cases. Then comes the more -- the finer, I mean, things. In other words, any bone, any single bone be the same type of bone or another bone that show an express juvenile trait that cannot be covered by the bones you have already counted, is one to be added. But there is no double counting there. It is not possible to double count. How would you? I mean, I still -- I mean, maybe it's me who doesn't understand, but it is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's leave aside your site-specific observations about Cerska. It's perfectly possible, isn't it, that at Nova Kasaba 99 all five of the people listed under the 13 to 17-year-old category were aged 15, 16, or 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. "Possible," in this context because so much is possible that I don't think that that moves the ball ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, with the greatest of respect, this is a criminal court where the burden of proof is on the Prosecution to prove matters beyond a reasonable doubt. And a possibility shifts that burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have been in criminal courts my whole life and this question of possibilities is -- is rarely allowed because most judges will say that most anything is possible. We don't do that objection here because it is a freer atmosphere, but I think at this point, at this time of the day, this is not moving the ball ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- because we're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. The site where the age-specific figures are entered it's probably refreshed your memory, are all the sites which you yourself exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Are you referring to page 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, page 8.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, no, these were sited exhumed by ICTY. Some of them by me, some of them by Wright, some of them about Haglund, some of them about Peccerelli, I guess. Yeah, as well. By everybody, pretty much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, you haven't understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I did not. Please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There is a list of all the sites exhumed by the ICTY. Some of them have a MMNI number in the -- next to one left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But not all of them have entries in the columns eight to 12, 13 to 17, 15 to 24, and 25 plus.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right. But maybe it is the time to explain what the MMNI is. Since we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think so. But, please, we've got five minutes to the break or a few minutes to the break. I want to carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, it is arguing with the witness who is trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are perfectly -- perfectly right. I know that we are running out of time. It's true. But on the other hand he was pointing to something that, in his mind, obviously, is very much relevant in trying to answer your question. So please let him. I know that it is defined in his report. We have an explanation what it is, but he is referring to a particular chart and I think he needs to go there. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have not touched upon what the MMNI is, and I think it is extremely relevant because otherwise we are going to cause a lot of confusion in this discussion. The point is that when I try to merge, to come up with an estimate, say -- okay. Since -- 1996 to 2001, how many people more or less have been, I mean, accounted for or remains have been dug. The issue becomes extremely complicated because, as I said, it is not a matter of just counting the MNI of each site. Then we would have a very charge number. It would be very easy, as a matter of fact, to count the MNI of each site, and we can say, okay this plus that plus that, and then we have X number. It doesn't make any sense. What we need to do first was to merge primary sites and secondary sites together. And then it was to calculate a minimal number of individuals based on all those sites to find a common element to all of those sites. By doing this, we would be making a lot of people invisible. Why invisible? Because, as I said before, some sites would combine, for example, the femur and would combine all the bones of other ages. Okay. But if we were looking for a common denominator to all the sites, we need to almost try to limit that to a maximum. And that is why we come up with this figure that you can see in page 7 of the same report. And that is that if we were to simply accounting the MNI of each site, we would come with a number of 2.691. As a matter of fact, by eliminating these possible, let's say, duplicates that would inflate the figure, we could come with the number of 2.541. So 2.541 is an ultraconservative approach to explain how many bodies or people - bodies should not be the term - people are accounted for by the remains recovered in all the exhumations between 1999 -- 1996 and 2001. I mean, I don't know whether that is clear, but that is extremely important. And that is why you will find a lot of missing slots in specific age categories. Not all the age categories were represented there. And what you have in page 8, as a matter of fact, is already we already merging existing data, the data that exists of course is not in the report, or the report will be a thousand pages with all the spread sheets. We are merging sites that are linked together, primary and secondary sites. So all the Glogova sites and Zeleni Jadar were all the same thing. People were put in a hole, then taken to another hole, but it is all the same bodies. So you -- you are not counting the bodies taken from the primary site on top of the ones of the primary site. Then you would be making up numbers. So what you have here is just a condensed merging of all the possible sites that are related. And by doing that I have omitted to put the specific figures per site. They do exist, of course. They are in the logs in the raw data I have used for the calculation. It does exist; it is not -- I have not made it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how many --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? Thank you. For the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many individuals were, in fact, exhumed at Hodzici Road 5?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not have a data with me here. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You do. It's on page 7.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry. That was my mistake. Yes, I do have it. 57. But Hodzici Road has 57 complete bodies, if I am not mistaken. Is a site that have almost complete bodies or complete bodies. 57, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many of them are age eight to 12?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That data I would not have here. I mean, that data does exist again but it is not -- hold on a second. Maybe I do have it in one of the previous reports. Then we can go back to the reports of 1999 and so on. Should be there. If you give me a moment, I will look for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise. I hate to intervene but we've two English speakers and I keep seeing the interpreters asking to slow down a little bit. I'm having a hard time following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Meek. What I suggest, Mr. Haynes, if you agree, is to have the break now. If we have the time -- the chance to refer to the other previous report that he has just hinted at. And we will reconvene in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I'm really I'm going to do my level best to make sure we finish with you today so that you can leave. So I've shortened things a little bit in that endeavour. But I'm going to look at this from a different angle, if I may. Is it your understanding that Dr. Haglund carried out a similar calculation to the minimum number of individuals to the one you have described, namely one which depends upon the counting of unique bones or one bone of a pair?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you, please, to have a look at our P00622. And it's page 62 of that document, and this is a report of Mr. Haglund about the exhumations at Branjevo military farm or Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, usher, could I provide the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that will speed up matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't read that. I don't know about the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps the easiest way is if I read it aloud slowly in English so that it be translated. It says, "The following section explains the methodology followed to estimate the minimum number of missing and/or unmatched body parts recovered from the Pilica grave site. For this purpose the presence of the following body parts was documented for all collection units: Crania, mandibles, necks, right and left denominant bones, upper and lower trunks, right and left arms, forearms and hands, and right and left legs, lower legs and feet. "In order to make this estimate it was necessary to standardise the data to the category of body part or limb. This process has introduced a factor of error in the final estimate of limbs with more than one bone, potentially inflating representation of forearms and lower legs. For example, one right radius and one right ulna were each considered to be two right forearms, although they could have been from the same individual. The estimate of crania, upper and lower thoraxes, mandibles, upper arms and legs, however, reflects the actual number of body parts at the site." "This method of calculation was necessary since body part inventories from two different sources were used. The first source was the list of missing body parts recorded by the pathologists in the autopsy report; the second from inventories of unassociated remains done by the anthropologists. In the former, there were different degrees of specification as to what bones were missing. The pathologists' description often referred to missing limbs without indicating side of the limb or whether the remains of at least one bone in that limb were present or not. Inventories of skeletal elements or body parts upon which these calculations of the minimum number --" could we move it up, please? "-- of individuals were based or presented in appendix E. The results of this analysis are now shown in table 8." Can we go over the page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There is table 8 indicating, as it were, a count of cranium, mandible, neck, upper trunk, lower trunk, right innominate, left innominate, right arm, left arm, right forearm, left forearm, right hand, left hand, and right leg. And he goes on then to make a summary of body parts missing. That's not the same system you've described, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, when reading it like this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's not age specific, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It does not mention age, no. It's just counting -- counting parts, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So would you agree that that's not the same method of calculating the minimum number of individuals that you employed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, you are completely right. I would say it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'm going to leave that there for just a moment to address just a small mathematical matter on your page 8 table, please, which is 02477. And I just want to look at the site listed at the very top line, Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you would be so good, please, as to total for me 9, 20, and 118?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It's like 148, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think it's 147. So how is it that 150 appears?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If you see the little number 4 next to the Cerska, there is a footnote that says, "Age data for three individuals missing."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: And this means that all these calculations here as they are concerned the MNI or the MMNI, are not using Haglund's, the same methodology, as I have just read it now, because, as I have told you, I have not read his reports, I just used the raw data. So I have recalculated, based on the raw data, these figures. That's why if there is data missing, I cannot, I mean, explain why or how, but there is data missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
