utterances.text: I will give an opportunity to explain to us. Why, in relation to I think 20 of the 30 sites, that are the subject of this investigation, we have no data as to the ages of the body parts used to calculate the minimum number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What do you mean there is no data on the ages of body parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why are the columns blank for the age groupings for Orahovac Lazete 2A, Orahovac Lazete 2C, Orahovac Lazete 1, Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 5, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Because, as I told I already, the data does exist, but this table is only merging things. So, for example, to answer your question, we can refer to a report of the 18th of June of 1999, okay. Where you can find it's called anthropological examination of human remains from Eastern Bosnia in 1998, where you will find the type of data you are referring to per site. But per site. In this other table we have merged those sites. So the data does exist, it is not simply depicted, not to have far too many numbers in the table and make it more difficult to read. That's simply why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's your answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to ask you a couple more things, please, about Dr. Haglund. And I wonder if we could put into e-court, please, P0611. And could we have page 43 of that document. I don't expect you to remember this, but this is a report in relation to the Cerska site which was exhumed between the 31st of July and the 22nd of August of 1996. And really, all I want to focus your attention on are the age groupings at figure 13.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we can see that Mr. Haglund's age groupings are less than 20, people in their 30s -- sorry, people in their 20s, people in their 30s, people in their 40s. Could we just go down a bit on the English, please. And people over the age of 50. Would you have said that they were wider or narrower groupings than you used?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would say that the 25 plus that I have is -- is more detailed in this case. 26 to 35, for example. 36 to 45, 45 plus. But if I may just comment, this -- but when seeing this I have -- I mean, I have an explanation, I mean obviously Dr. Haglund will be the one explaining his own report, but, I mean, my understanding is also very context based. Let's just for a moment go back to 1996, from what I recall. When we started the first site, Cerska, all the bodies were complete, 150 of them, you know? Complete cadavers. With complete cadavers you can be as complete and detailed as you can be. Having a whole cadaver you can have different indicators and you can have different ways of separating, creating age ranges. You know. But again don't lose sight of one thing. When you see this pie chart, this is the way that Haglund is presenting data that does exist in each autopsy report. This doesn't mean that all the cases, I mean case-by-case where aged 16 to 25, maybe it was one person 16 to 19, or 16 to 20s. It was fitted into that interval. So, yes, it is a different way to present it, but maybe, you know, I'm speculating there, it is also based on the fact that when we started work in 1996, we were dealing with complete corpses and having that you can, you know, have different degrees of accuracy in your age intervals, how you present it. It's a possible. I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you ought to have the opportunity to look at pages 34 and 35 of this report, please. [Microphone not activated]. These are remains covered -- recovered from Cerska. They're not complete bodies, are they?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, what I see here, can I see the femur down there, figure 9? No. I mean, I don't think that these -- the interpretation I think it incorrect. I think that this is a case of somebody who has been shot through the leg and maybe through the mandible. I mean, they are aspects of the same body. Why they have taken pictures separately or not, I mean, there is nothing I can answer, I mean, on behalf of anybody, but what I see here is the case code is the same, CSK-52, and that we have a fractured mandible and we have a fractured -- I mean, right femur. You know, that's pretty much it. I mean, whether -- I mean, that's it. I mean, just fractured bones from the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to move on to one last thing, and I need into e-court, please, P00616 at page 41. Now, this is the report relating to Lazete 2, which was excavated in September of 1996, going into October. So commenced, as it were, immediately after Cerska, the report of which we've just been looking at. And we can see now Mr. Haglund's age groupings are 11 to 15, 16 to 25, 26 to 35, 36 to 45, 45 plus. And these are the age groupings he says should be subject to a plus one/minus one error count, as it were. Again, would you say they were more specific groups than you used or less specific?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Hold on a second. We are confusing two things here. Again, these are the age groupings to fit data into. This is not the individual estimates to which this plus minus one standard deviation as he mentioned in the report are presented. I mean, they are two different things. Okay. I mean, let's be very clear. I already explained you that, but I'm repeating it here. The issue of the standard deviation he mentioned whatever regarding one -- the individual estimate is one thing. This is the distribution of ages meaning the individual ages put into some kind of thing to be -- to be -- to picture it, you know, to have like a normal distribution, whatsoever. That's simply completely different. This age ranges are -- yes, they are different. But at the same time they are at -- at the same time they are comparable. By the same token I would tell you that the -- the 25 below compares to the A to 25 category, we merge them all together. And the 25 plus encompasses the 26 to 45 plus. They are just different ways of expressing very much the same thing, with a different degree of, let's say, accuracy or precision, in this case. This looks more precise. But maybe depended also on the type of body parts we are dealing with, in the completeness of the remains, a number of factors. What I do know is that from 1998 onwards, without -- specifically 1998, with such a volume, such an amount of body parts that, if I'm not mistaken, at the mortuary at one point in time we had like over 5.000 cases, I mean cases, it could be a hand, a foot, a whatever. I mean, therefore your level of accuracy and precision would be completely different than this. That is, I mean, an educated opinion, what I'm giving you, after the clarification I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I really am doing my best to finish quickly and I've just got a couple more questions about this. This, of course, is a completely different set of age groupings from that used by Mr. Haglund in the report he wrote in relation to Cerska, isn't it, where he had under 20, 20s, 30s, 40s, and over 50s?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. At this point we're getting into reports he's not read and apples and oranges, and I think Haglund is here for that. And I don't know where we're going with questions like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can finish it off very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you regard a change in the basis of, as it were, the groupings you placed on bodies and body parts as being systematic?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I don't think I follow your question. I mean, could you rephrase it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be a good system for Mr. Haglund to have adopted a consistent base of age groupings?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I mean I can give you -- I can give you a personal opinion, but that's just a matter of speculation. I mean, yes, everything -- I mean would have been done, I mean, better, would have been good. But if it's -- we really in the area of speculation. It is very conditional. I mean, if so many other factors would be taken into account. That is -- yet again is a question you may pose to Dr. Haglund in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm posing it to you because, as you've agreed with me, age determination and grouping of ages is very important for the whole calculation. But I'm going leave it there. Thank you very much for answering all my questions and I do hope you have a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Point of clarification. Earlier today you testified, and I can get it real quick, that during your work in Srebrenica case in 1996 they asked you what position you held, your answer was, "from a UN point of view, I was a junior forensic anthropologist or forensic expert employed by the Tribunal. There were two people of technical expertise at the Tribunal at the time. It was Dr. Bill Haglund and myself. Now, who -- both you and Haglund were junior forensic anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, the seniority, I would say -- the seniority is reflected by the type of post, I would say, that each of us had. Certainly I had a junior post as concerned my -- my UN status, my -- my professional level, if I be more precise. But to be even more precise, remember that in 1996, technically, and I can speak for myself, again, I do not know the contractual details of anything. I was employed by ICTR. I was on loan to ICTY. So I was part of the ICTE [sic], the Arusha, the international tribunal -- the other -- on the African side. There was -- paid by them while working in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So, sir, would it be a fair statement then that Haglund was the senior advisor in the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was the senior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after the end of 1997 or 1998, isn't it a fact that the ICTY severed their connections with the group called Physicians for Human Rights, which Haglund was a member of, and was -- when he was doing this work as a senior forensic anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is my understanding that from 1997 onwards, the decision was taken by the Tribunal to run its own operations, say, in-house, so that would recruiting directly people, setting up the teams directly and not through -- I mean, third parties like Physicians for Human Rights at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. That was my next question: Once that relationship was severed with the PHR, the ICTY did form their own in-house forensic team and it was directed by you, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I was a person who assembled the teams, but already in 1997 the -- Richard Wright at the time was employed under the same, I mean, arrangement with a direct contract with the Tribunal as being the senior archaeologist for the site, and there was also a chief pathologist employed and I, as being the in-house forensic person, undertook the position of chief anthropologist, I mean, at the mortuary at that time, although I was working in the field or mortuary, depending where I was needed pretty much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you a member or have you ever been a member of the group PHR, Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you a member of ABFA, I think -- I believe you know who -- what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The American Board of Physical Anthropology of the American Academy of Forensic Sciences?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm not -- I'm not American.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, that the highest degree of accreditation from that ABFA would be to be a diplomat?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Meaning -- rephrase the thing. In order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You want me to rephrase it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I think I can answer your question, but let me rephrase the answer I was thinking to give you. The American Academy of Forensic Sciences have a board, the forensic anthropology board, the people take a board exam for which you need to have a Ph.D. That's number one. It is a qualification that is - I am not mistaken on a -- that one - taken by North Americans, so for time being that I may be wrong, there is like 50 diplomats or maybe less, of which one is Canadian and the other ones are of -- I mean U.S. nationality. So, yes, those are the requisites for -- for -- yes, for -- yes, you have to be pretty much from the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Mr. Baraybar, are you ware that Mr. Haglund is not a diplomat of the American Board of Forensic Anthropology?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I noticed that -- I'm going to ask you a few questions about colleagues of yours: But he is an American, correct, Haglund?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I guess so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you a few questions. Do you know or have you worked with a Tom -- Tom Grow, G-r-o-w, MD?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Now, we are getting to -- an orthopaedic surgeon, maybe? 1996, you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Practicing as an radiologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you know him very well?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I mean, I'm -- that's my own pre-history, in a way. That's 11 years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We're going to have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I guess so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How about Patrick Myers, an archaeologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Patrick Myers, yes, I do remember very well. He was an archaeologist, an American archaeologist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he competent, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: He is very competent. I lost track of him long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. How about Dorothy Gallagher, another anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Dorothy Gallagher was an anthropologist at Baton Rouge, could that be? LSU maybe, Louisiana State University? I think she was a student of Mary Mannheim. I mean, I -- that I don't recall. However she went there as data -- as a data entry person. That is what I do recall. Yes. She was not doing cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall working with her back then in 1996?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: She was a very nice person, but she was not doing cases. She was there to type things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about David del Pino, a Chilean anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, David Pino, yes, I remember. I lost sight of him also in those days, 1996 or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And was he a competent anthropologist, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: He was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to work with a John Gerns, G-e-r-n-s, he was an administrator?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Was he competent, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: He is -- yes, I mean he -- again he was not an archaeologist or anthropologist or anything of the kind. I think he is a former air force medical examiner or something of the kind. I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you wouldn't consider these people that I have just mentioned to you to be like junior helpers in this project in 1996, would you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, it all depends how -- I mean how we define them, really. Helpers. Patrick Myers, for example, was a person that was not really helping in the way I would understand it. Meaning helping would be an assistant, somebody, you know, carrying things without any responsibility. Patrick Myers was somebody who was actually working in the hole, in the grave, and who was extremely competent, and I would not see him as a helper. I would see Dorothy Gallagher as a helper, maybe, as somebody typing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, and I appreciate that. So besides -- besides Dorothy Gallagher, the rest you would categorise just like you did Patrick Myers, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, remember there were people coming from different backgrounds but they had different experience back in their own countries but I think they were relevant, in a way, to -- to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you know Fredy Peccerelli, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you know Fredy testified here yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I asked Fredy Peccerelli a question, in your field -- in his field and your field as a forensic anthropologist who he believed to be the foremost pioneer in that area in the world, and I'm going to ask you the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, we all have a -- I think that -- I mean, I'm doing mind reading here but we all have a common -- I mean, a common denominator, I think for us pose [sic], that would be Clyde Snow. As you know, Clyde Snow is an American anthropologist and -- who is very much one of the people who pioneered the application of forensic anthropologist to human rights violation cases starting in Argentina, and he fathered teams all over, including the Guatemalans, of course, and lately the Peruvian team that I am part of as well. So, I mean, Clyde is kind of like father figure, I mean, field -- in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I notice in your CV that in 1997 you presented a paper in a conference and it was on Haiti, Rwanda, and the Balkans at the crossroads of Science and Experience. You did that at the department of anthropology University of Oklahoma in Norman, on March 6th. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you do that with Clyde Snow?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, but I did other things with Clyde Snow I mean, regarding case work for example, that I do not even know. That I did not know. I mean, this CV is very old. We actually did a case, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to interrupt you. I really -- I apologise but I know you that you need to get home for personal reasons, and I just want to get this finished as quickly as possible. Yesterday we heard from -- frankly, let me just ask you this question. Wasn't it Clyde Snow who recommended you to the United Nations for the in-house job, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, that I do not know. As far -- and as far as I know, remember I was in Haiti, I mean, before that, so I came from Haiti to Rwanda. So not as far -- not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. We heard yesterday from your colleague Fredy Peccerelli that in his opinion the finalisation of the cause and manner of death is something that only experts have to determine. Experts in your area would be the pathologist and forensic anthropologist. Am I correct? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you also agree that it would be improper to have a defence lawyer or any lawyer participate in the finalisation of the manner and cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell me why, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, primarily because, I mean, I do not know -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am going to object to this. Unless there is a factual showing of what he is talking about and the relevance to this, this is -- this question is just a complete vacuum. But -- I mean, how does a defence lawyer get involved -- these -- I mean, I'll stipulate the defence lawyers are not experts and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He said all lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I said all lawyers, judge. Any lawyer is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Let him answer the question because I think -- yeah, but he was being asked to specify why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primarily because a lawyer is not a specialist in those kind of -- of matters. I mean, it is set -- likewise it would be the reverse. I mean, a pathologist, anthropologist discussing on the verdicts or legal things for which we have no competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, very quickly, I would ask you, what role, if any, did the Office of the Prosecutor or any of his team of investigators play in determining age, if any, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, like a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And Jose, let me ask you this: Can you remember, did at any time you -- were you ever given a briefing or a background by the OTP such as that, when you go to look for these graves, you are going to find mostly men, mostly military-aged men, most of them will be civilians, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. We were just pointed at -- as stated in the reports, for example, shown an aerial photograph with a stain of dirt, as seen from above and with a date on it and we have to just try to see the grave or not. I mean, who is there, how, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Jose, one last question. I understand that -- Mr. Baraybar, excuse me. I understand that at one point during your work in the Srebrenica grave sites that you became ill. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Back in 1996, if I'm not mistaken. I had surgery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact, sir, that you had some abdominal pains and that you told Bill Haglund about these abdominal pains? Yes or no. I'm just -- I'm trying to finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the relevancy of this. This is -- what's -- we're gearing up for this witch hunt, which will happen tomorrow, but I think we can stop it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. What's the relevance of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, the relevance is, Judge -- is obviously as to the competence of -- of Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the way he supervised, because I think Mr. Baraybar has already testified that he was the main supervisor in this group, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was the supervisor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The very simple question is, didn't he tell you were gold bricking and wouldn't even give you a ride? You had to talk several miles to even get to a hospital where you had surgery?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I did not walk to the hospital, but I cannot recall the exact -- I mean, there was some argument of some kind. I couldn't really tell you what he told me or whatever, but there was a bit of an argument there, I mean -- or something of the kind. That's what I recall. I mean, I'm not lying to you, I would not -- I do not recall exactly, you know, what he told me or told him or whatever. But the fact is, yes, I did have surgery; yes, I had abdominal pain; yes, I ended up in a military hospital or whatever for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, yes, you had to walk some ways to get there?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, no, I did not walk to the hospital, but, I mean, that I don't -- that I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Enough of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, if you have further questions on any other subject, any other topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, would you agree that the residue of earth or the material that we find on the bodies could indicate the location at which the victim actually died?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If we are referring to soil found with the bodies, meaning in secondary sites, what the soil coming -- associated to the bodies will tell you is the provenance of the bodies, not the place where they died. I mean that -- I -- no. I mean, is -- where they were buried but not when they died. I mean, that's two different things. An interruption, please. Can I -- since she speaks French, can I actually listen to her question in French because the -- the -- sorry. I mean, and I respond in French with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problems with that. You're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's only because of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, you can follow in French, but preferably if you can answer in English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. I will, I will. Okay, so I will listen in French and answer in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that at one of the sites that you located, the soil samples were taken and analysed and showed that the victims were in a place where cereals had been cultivated before they died.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean, yes -- I mean, that is -- that is correct. I mean, are you referring to this meadow, I think it's Sandici meadow, because the meadow have been cultivation of maize and other cereals, and the inference is if people did die in this specific case, I mean, of course it is correct. I mean, with an example I can answer. Since people, I mean, die there and the bodies were taken, mechanically lifted from there, they were taken with the soil as well. And buried in a place with that soil. So in that specific case, and there will be a relationship between, let's say, the place of death and -- and the soil of that place going to the place where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And there was also the site where you discovered that victims had been killed. That was in the vicinity of -- of a tree?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct. And you are referring to one of the Nova Kasaba sites. Now, a reconstruction is the most probable scenario that can explain why and how some of these branches and leaves from this willow tree ended up in the grave intermixed with bodies, considering that the tree itself was like 200 metres away from the location. They were not just leaves taken by the wind, but actually branches. So we did a bit of an experiment that is explained in one of reports and we concluded that the most probable -- probable explanation for those leaves and branches in the grave was that the bodies were collected from a location close to the tree and -- and the tree was shaken, the branches and leaves fell on the bodies and then they were taken to the grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also worked on a site where the bodies were bodies for which you established a link with the warehouse in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'll go back to my question, my initial question about the examples that I've just provided you with. Would you agree that in fact one could establish on the basis of the samples found in the mass graves the sites where the victims were before their deaths or the sites where they may have been killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I mean in -- in that context and with those explanations, yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As far as you know, was a link ever established between the victims who had been found at the sites that you worked on and the UNPROFOR base at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was such a link ever established between the sites that you worked at and the places that were apparently within the town of Bratunac? I'm referring to the town of Bratunac itself. I'm not referring to the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. On behalf of the Tribunal. Yes, I wouldn't imagine there is a redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I assure you there wouldn't be any questions from our side. So, Witness, that brings your testimony to an end. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have three minutes. Are we to anticipate any major objections to the list of exhibits that the Prosecution is proposing to tender? No. Okay. So that now we can go through this list. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's my understanding that there's just a couple of details, three items that have not been previously entered. The first one is P01606, and that was something that -- well, it was -- I won't get into -- that was referred to a -- oh, in another -- I believe it was in his previous testimony. So we wanted to put that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then P02477, that's the minimal number of individuals which I had referred to, came in in the last trial through Dean Manning. And so that wasn't the subject of the 92 bis motion. And then finally PIC 00076, the little drawing that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any objections to any of the documents appearing in the list that has been circulated? None. So they are so admitted. Any one of the Defence teams, particularly you, Mr. Haynes, wish to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The only documents that I put to the witness will come into evidence through other witnesses anyway, so I'm not going to tender them as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much. So tomorrow we start with Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and he is our last -- we don't have another witness based on the estimates, but we -- so that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And we'll try to finish with his testimony tomorrow. I think we have a revised estimate of three hours on the part of the Defence. So have a nice evening. We stand adjourned until tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
